That catches a repeat the summed table never saw: the shared feature axis keeps features outside the mass range, so a spectrum that resamples to nothing still fills the mobility table. A builder that knows of a repeat sums it with the same chunked sort and merge the summed table uses. A source with no repeat pays nothing.

What changes in a store. Only sources that reach the standalone passes and measure some position twice. Today those are imzML files with a mobility array: their _mobility table's X holds one entry per (row, column), so X.nnz drops by the repeated entries. The dense values do not change. A Bruker .tdf read through the vendor library always takes the fused route and does not change. No shipped reader feeds the MS/MS table from the standalone passes, so no _msms table changes.

Known limits.

  • No real source with a repeated position was converted for this entry. The synthetic iprm-PASEF copy has a spot holding two frames, but the two share no grid cell and it writes no MS/MS table, so it stores the same either way.
  • The MS/MS builder relies on the converter's count alone, because a row legitimately arrives once per precursor there. A repeat the summed table does not count would still be stored twice. No shipped reader reaches that builder outside the fused route.

docs.title: D41. A plane's table holds the mass-mobility heatmap of its own plane
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13). Removes the second known limit of D38 (the heatmap of a multi-plane store covering every plane).

Decision. A multi-slice source converted as 2D writes one table per z plane. Each of them now holds, in uns["mobility_heatmap"], the heatmap of its own plane's pixels: the same pixels its uns["average_spectrum"] averages over. The one raw mobility pass the conversion already made builds every plane's heatmap, routing each pixel by its z. Under D38 each plane's heatmap then divides by the distinct positions on that plane, which are the rows its table holds. A volume (--handle-3d) and a single-plane source keep one heatmap over every pixel, which is again the population of their one table.

Why. Since #243 a plane's average_spectrum is its own plane's mean. The heatmap beside it was still built once over every plane, and every plane's table was handed the same dictionary. current_ratio was then written into that shared dictionary once per table, comparing the dataset-wide heatmap with that plane's mean, so the store kept the last plane's ratio in every table. A two-plane source whose second plane is three times brighter, converted from the raw sum (scan_sum), showed it:

Table Stored ratio, before Ratio of its own table, before Now z0 0.6667 2.0 1.0 z1 0.6667 0.6667 1.0

The heatmap's total was 47 in both tables, against plane means of 23.5 and 70.5. docs/output-format.md promised the marginal equals the average_spectrum beside it under scan_sum, and it held on no plane.

The objection. Keep one dataset-wide heatmap, give each table its own copy, and compute the ratio against a dataset-wide mean. It did not win. That mean is stored nowhere since #243, so the ratio would compare against a number no reader of the store can see, and the marginal would still differ from the spectrum it is drawn beside. A viewer showing one plane's ion image next to a heatmap of every plane misleads the same way the old shared mean spectrum did. average_spectrum_per_region stays dataset-wide for a different reason: a region has no z (see docs/output-format.md), whereas every pixel the heatmap reads has one.

Cost. One accumulator per plane while the pass runs: about 8 MB per plane at the default 4,000 m/z bins by 256 mobility channels. The point buffer (up to 4 million points, 64 MB) is folded in whenever the pass moves to another plane, so only one plane holds one at a time, as before. No extra read; the stub conversion in the tests still makes one mobility pass for two planes. A plane whose pixels yield no mobility spectra gets no heatmap, and the conversion says so at WARNING.

What changes in a store. Stores of multi-slice sources with an ion mobility dimension converted as 2D: each plane's mobility_heatmap.counts becomes that plane's mean frame, and current_ratio becomes that plane's ratio (1.0 under scan_sum). Each plane's table stores its own block where before all held the same values. Volumes, single-plane sources (every Bruker TDF) and sources without mobility do not change.

docs.title: D42. A store records a SHA-256 of its mass axis
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13).

Decision. Every converted store records msi_metadata.provenance.mass_axis, an object with two members: sha256 and n_bins. sha256 is the SHA-256 of the main MSI table's var["mz"], taken as little-endian float64 bytes whatever dtype the array is held or written in, as lower-case hex. n_bins is the number of values. It is written whether or not the conversion resampled. There is one value per store: the sibling tables (_mobility, _msms) carry the main table's value, because their mz_index points into that axis (D6), not because their own var["mz"] hashes to it.

Why. Showing that two stores share an axis needed both arrays loaded and compared. The recorded settings do not answer it: a tof law is filled from detection, numpy and the platform can change a float, and a --no-resample conversion has no resampling step to read a setting from. A later plan of one axis for several sources (issue #449) has to check a conversion against that axis, and a hash is the cheapest thing to check against.

Where it lives and why. In provenance, which is versioned and validated, and which every store has. Not on the "mass axis resampling" processing step: that step is absent under --no-resample, and the axis exists all the same. Not in the root attributes or in uns["essential_metadata"]: both are outside the versioned, validated schema, so a validator could not check the value. The field is optional, so a standalone document, which has no axis, stays valid without it. It is not bound to a CV term: MS:1003151 (SHA-256) names a file checksum, and this is a hash of an array. The gap is listed in CANDIDATE_CV_CONCEPTS.

What changes in a store. Every new store gains provenance.mass_axis, and the schema version is 0.11.0. No other value changes. Stores written earlier are unchanged and still valid. thyra validate recomputes the hash from var["mz"] of each plain MSI table that has the field and reports an error at provenance.mass_axis when it differs; a store without the field gets no such check.

Known limits.

  • The hash is of the bits. Two axes that differ by one ulp are two axes. This is intended: the use is to show that two stores are bin for bin the same.
  • When the msi_metadata block cannot be built, which is logged, the store carries no fingerprint.
  • Sibling tables carry the main axis's value, not the hash of their own var["mz"] (D6).
  • thyra validate checks every plain table that records the field. A table added to a store later, with a different var["mz"] and a copy of the main table's block, fails that check. Its block must drop or replace the field.
  • The field is not a CV term.

docs.title: D43. A plan fixes one mass axis for several sources
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13). Amended by D56 (2026-10-16).

Decision. plan_mass_axis(sources) reads each source's header, as preview_msi does, and returns a MassAxisPlan. The plan holds the axis settings only: the axis type, the range, the bin width at one reference m/z (or, for a tof axis, the width law and the bins per peak width), the bin count, and the D42 fingerprint of the axis those settings lay. The resampling method is not part of the axis (AxisPlan), so each conversion keeps its own detector's method unless the caller forces one in the plan. The plan decides each setting the caller leaves open:

  • The range is the intersection of the sources' ranges.
  • The width is the widest width any source's detector declares (else the axis type's default), each first stated at the reference m/z under the axis law (width grows as m^0 on constant, m^0.5 on linear_tof, m^1 on reflector_tof, m^1.5 on orbitrap, m^2 on fticr).
  • The plan is refused when the ranges have no m/z in common, when the detectors want different axis types, and when tof sources declare different width laws. A caller's value is used as given.

A conversion given a plan builds the axis from the plan's settings and refuses, before reading any spectrum, when the fingerprint of the axis it built differs from the plan's.

Why. Comparing two stores bin for bin needs one var["mz"] for both. Five settings rebuild the axis, and the D42 fingerprint proves they did. The width is the widest because, on an axis finer than a source's own peaks, that source's centroids scatter over neighbouring bins from pixel to pixel and one ion becomes several features. A coarser axis costs the finer source resolution instead, and the plan names it in a warning. The range is the intersection so that every bin is measured in every store.

What changes in a store. Nothing. A plan only picks settings that already exist. The new check refuses a conversion; it writes nothing.

Known limits.

  • An imzML range is the span of the data observed, not the acquisition window, so an intersection bound set by an imzML source may cut signal near the edge. The plan warns. An mzPeak range is observed data too when the archive states no scan window, but that cannot be told from the header cheaply, so it is not flagged.
  • The source with the finer width loses resolution on the shared axis, and under tic_preserving bins coarser than a source's own can merge narrow peaks (#442). D50 fixes the second part.
  • There is no plan for "the axis of an existing store" yet.

docs.title: D44. Only a reader that can select a region accepts the region option
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13). Superseded in part by D57 (2026-10-16): one region now gives a region map, so a single-region store keeps the source's region number and name. Superseded in part by D83 (2026-10-22): the Waters reader selects a region too, and the gate is a reader attribute (selects_regions), not a timsTOF check.

Decision. region selects one region, and only the timsTOF reader can do that. Every other reader refuses it, through the API as well as the CLI. The refusal lives in BaseMSIReader, so a new reader refuses it until it learns to honour it. thyra.list_regions(path) lists the regions of any input from its header: each region's number, .mis Area name, spectrum count and box. Two readers record more than before:

  • Rapiflex builds a region map from the position log. A spot named R{n}X{x}Y{y} is region n, at its raster cell minus the .dat header origin. The name is the n-th .mis Area, the pairing D31 already uses. As on timsTOF, one region gives no map.
  • solariX adds each region's bounds to its region summary, in the store's pixel grid, as timsTOF and mzPeak give them.

Why. solariX, Rapiflex, imzML, PHI and Waters dropped region in silence through the API, and converted every region of an input the caller asked to cut. On mzPeak the CLI logged it as ignored and the reader then refused it. One rule gives one message. A caller who wants one store per region needs the region list first, and had to open the vendor database to get it. list_regions always returns at least one entry, so a loop over it works on any input; MsiPreview.regions stays None for one region, which answers a different question.

What changes in a store.

  • A multi-region Rapiflex store: obs["region_number"] holds the position-log region instead of 1 everywhere, uns["regions"] has one entry per region with n_spectra, bounds and name, and uns["average_spectrum_per_region"] appears. A single-region Rapiflex store is unchanged.
  • A solariX store: each entry of uns["regions"] and of format_specific.regions gains bounds.
  • A call that passed region to another format now fails instead of writing a store of the whole input.

Known limits.

  • The Rapiflex keying was checked on one real single-region acquisition, where every position-log spot landed on its offset-table cell. No multi-region Rapiflex acquisition was available. When a spectrum has no position-log spot, or a cell is in two regions, the reader warns and writes no map.
  • solariX regions have no names. The positional Area pairing is not verified on solariX.
  • n_spectra counts spectra, not pixels: a position measured twice (D40) counts twice.
  • Region selection for solariX, Rapiflex and mzPeak, which know their regions, is not part of this decision.

docs.title: D45. The metadata block names the sample and the spectrum representation
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13).

Decision. Schema 0.12.0 adds three optional facts to msi_metadata:

  • sample.sample_id (MS:1000001 sample number) and sample.sample_name (MS:1000002 sample name). Only the person converting fills them, through convert_msi(sample_id=..., sample_name=...) or --sample-id. Thyra never reads them from the source.
  • ms_analysis.spectrum_representation, "profile" or "centroid", with its term (MS:1000128 / MS:1000127, under MS:1000525 spectrum representation). It is the representation the reader delivered, the same fact uns["essential_metadata"]["spectrum_type"] records. That key stays.

The Bruker timsTOF extractor now states the representation too. It used to state none. TSF is centroid (the vendor line spectrum, D1). TDF read with vendor_centroid is centroid. TDF read with scan_sum, the default, is profile: the summed digitizer indices are unpicked and equal Bruker's own quasi-profile export (D1), the same reasoning that labels PHI profile.

Why. Code that combines stores of one study had two problems. Whether two stores can be combined depended on the spectrum representation, which sat outside the versioned block. For example, profile and centroid stores should not share a tic_preserving axis. And the stores could be told apart only by a file path, which is not a sample. The Provenance docstring said the root attributes recorded the representation; they never did. That text is corrected.

Where it lives and why. The representation sits in ms_analysis, beside polarity, because it describes the acquired spectra. Resampling does not change it: Thyra never picks peaks (D1), and the resampling step is recorded in processing. The sample fields sit in sample, the section METASPACE and SDRF both use for sample identity.

What is left unset. An imzML file that declares neither MS:1000127 nor MS:1000128 gets a guess: processed mode is taken as centroid, with a warning. The guess still picks the resampling method, and it is still written to uns["essential_metadata"]["spectrum_type"]. The block leaves the field unset, by the builder's rule that unset beats guessed. The sample fields are never filled from a vendor SampleName, an imzML sample list, or dataset_id. Any of these can hold a placeholder or a person's identifier, and the block is copied into every metadata document Thyra writes.

Objection that did not win. "Take the sample from the file." Bruker GlobalMetadata.SampleName and imzML sampleList exist, but both hold free text typed at the instrument or written by the exporting software, which can be a placeholder or a person's identifier. Promoting that text into a field named "sample id" would present it as a curated identifier.

What changes in a store. Every new store has schema version 0.12.0 and ms_analysis.spectrum_representation wherever the reader states one. Bruker timsTOF stores also gain uns["essential_metadata"]["spectrum_type"], which was None. Their resampling defaults do not change when the instrument name is read: the timsTOF detector matches on it before any spectrum type is consulted. A .d whose name cannot be read, or lacks "timsTOF", used to fall to the default detector (constant axis). Read as centroid (TSF, or TDF with vendor_centroid), it now reaches the centroid detector, whose reflector-TOF axis is the one the timsTOF detector would have chosen. When the Bruker library cannot centroid, the reader falls back to scan_sum with a warning; the processing step and the representation now say scan_sum and profile, where the step used to repeat the request. A store converted with a sample id or name carries them in sample. Stores written earlier are unchanged and still valid.

Known limits.

  • One conversion names one sample, even when the slide holds several regions. Each region has its own name in uns["regions"].
  • The sample id and name are stored as typed. Thyra cannot tell a patient identifier from a code, so the documentation says not to use one.
  • thyra metadata and the preview read a timsTOF .d with the default scan_sum, and an imzML without --spectrum-type. Their document can therefore differ from what a conversion with other options stores.

docs.title: D46. A processed imzML with mobility gets the heatmap, and the grid when asked
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13). Amended by D82 (2026-10-22).

Decision. The range a per-pixel mobility source is binned over is the smallest and largest finite mobility value it holds. A reader states it through one method, get_mobility_value_range(). A source with a shared axis (Bruker TDF, a continuous imzML export) reads it off the axis values, as before. An imzML whose pixels carry their own mobility values (processed mode, as TIMSCONVERT writes it, or a continuous file whose arrays differ) reads it in one pass over its mobility arrays, and only those arrays, the first time anything asks. The result is cached, so the heatmap and the grid get the same two numbers. From this:

  • Such a file gets uns["mobility_heatmap"] by default, like every other mobility source (D3).
  • --mobility-grid, --mobility-bins, --mobility-min and --mobility-max are accepted on imzML. On a per-pixel file they write {table}_mobility with the grid's contract: uns["mobility_grid"], 256 channels on the heatmap's own edges, and uns["mobility_marginal"].
  • On a continuous file with a shared axis the table is read off the shared features, as before. --mobility-grid is ignored there, and a WARNING now says so.
  • A point whose mobility value is not a finite number has no channel. The imzML reader leaves it out of the mobility point cloud and says how many at WARNING. The summed table keeps it.

Why. Before this, a processed imzML with a mobility array kept no mobility at all. The log told the user to pass --mobility-grid, and the CLI then called that flag ignored on imzML. Processed mode is how TIMSCONVERT writes timsTOF imaging data, and a recent review of ion mobility imaging names unread mobility in such files as a bottleneck of the field (doi:10.1021/acsmeasuresciau.6c00282). Nothing in the converter was specific to TDF except where the range came from.

The range comes from the values because only they are sure to contain every point. TDF uses its values for the same reason: its per-scan 1/K0 overhangs the declared acquisition range. PSI-MS has terms for a lowest and highest observed mobility (MS:1003437, MS:1003438), but Thyra reads neither, and a stated range narrower than the data would pile points into an edge channel.

Objections considered.

  • A whole extra read for a range. It reads the mobility arrays only: a third of a 64-bit .ibd. The heatmap itself is already one more full pass on any source other than TDF. --no-mobility-heatmap without a grid reads nothing extra.
  • A range stated in the file would be free. It would be, when present and right. Neither can be checked without reading the values.

What changes in a store.

  • A processed imzML (or a continuous one with differing arrays) with a mobility array: the summed table gains uns["mobility_heatmap"]. uns["mobility_axis"] is unchanged and records no range: the range is in the heatmap's mobility_edges and the grid's edges.
  • The same file with --mobility-grid: a {table}_mobility table, its uns["mobility_grid"] and uns["mobility_marginal"], uns["mobility_axis"]["resolved_table"] on the summed table, and msi_metadata.ms_analysis.ion_mobility.grid. When the array states 1/K0 in MS:1002814, the table also carries var["ccs"] and uns["ccs"], as every 1/K0 mobility table does (D47). That lifts the last known limit D47 lists.
  • A continuous imzML whose shared mobility axis holds a non-finite value: the heatmap was refused with an error before (the channel index was undefined) and is now written without those points.
  • Bruker TDF and continuous imzML with a finite shared axis: nothing.

Known limits.

  • The grid's marginal reproduces the summed table only when the summed table puts the same points on their nearest bin: no resampling, or nearest_neighbor. Under tic_preserving it does not. On a resampled axis a point exactly at the data's m/z edge can also lie just outside the first or last bin centre; the heatmap and the grid drop it while the summed table folds it into the edge bin (#347). current_ratio records both. D52 lifts the second part: the heatmap and the grid now keep the points the summed table keeps.
  • A multi-plane imzML converted as 2D reads the whole file once per plane for the grid's discovery pass.
  • With --no-resample the raw union axis times 256 channels can pass the grid's size ceiling (D4).

docs.title: D47. A 1/K0 mobility table carries each feature's CCS, for charge 1
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13). Reverses the rule, stated in the code since the CCS function shipped in v3.13.0, that the converter never writes a cross section.

Decision. A mobility table whose axis is 1/K0 in V s/cm2 carries var["ccs"]: each feature's collision cross section in square angstroms, float64. It is computed from the feature's own mz and mobility by the Mason-Schamp equation, for a charge of 1, in nitrogen (28.0134 Da) at 305 K. The same table carries uns["ccs"], which records the quantity and unit (MS:1002954, UO:0000324), the method, the assumed charge, the gas, its mass and the temperature, and that these conditions are a convention. Keys are plain names and accessions are values, as in the other uns blocks. One function adds both, where the two mechanisms that fill the table meet, so a continuous imzML export and a TDF grid, per plane or as a volume, all get them. The schema reserves the column name (0.13.0); the document is unchanged.

The axis must say it is 1/K0 (MS:1002815) and that its unit is MS:1002814. A drift-time axis gets neither the column nor the block. Neither does an axis whose quantity or unit is not stated.

Why. A cross section is what IM-MSI work compares across instruments and against libraries. 1/K0 depends on the gas, the temperature and the calibration; a CCS is meant to be the ion's own. Every consumer of a TIMS table would otherwise repeat the same conversion with the same assumptions, and some would get the constants wrong: 28.013 Da instead of 28.0134 already moves the result by 7e-6, and 304.85 K instead of 305 K by 2.5e-4.

Where the conditions come from. From the convention, not from the run. Bruker's tims_oneoverk0_to_ccs_for_mz takes no gas or temperature; it uses nitrogen at 305 K, and the formula reproduces it with these two values. The TDF holds no drift-gas or temperature field that Thyra reads: GlobalMetadata gives the 1/K0 range, TimsCalibration gives unnamed coefficients, and the mobility keys of CalibrationInfo are zero on the one imaging TDF read. conditions_source: "convention" says so, so a reader does not take the values for the run's conditions.

Why the formula, never the vendor library. The same formula fills the column on every route and every platform, so a store does not depend on whether the machine's library exports the conversion. The library also converts one value per call, which is millions of calls on a grid table. The two agree to 1e-6 relative from m/z 100 up and to 2.2e-6 at m/z 50, measured on the synthetic TDF and on a probe from m/z 50 to 3000. The gap grows as the ion gets lighter and no single gas mass removes it.

The charge. MALDI ions are almost always singly charged, and no source states a feature's charge. Recording 1 as an assumption, in the block beside the values, is not the same as storing a value the source does not state (the objection D30 answers): the column is derived, and the block says from what. A consumer who knows a feature is doubly charged recomputes it with mason_schamp_ccs. The stored value cannot be rescaled, because the charge also changes the ion's mass in the reduced mass.

Alternatives.

  • No column; leave it to consumers. The previous rule. It keeps the store free of an assumption, but every consumer repeats the conversion and chooses its own constants, so two tools give two answers for one store. The function was already public and tested; the gap was that nobody had to call it.
  • A per-feature charge column. Honest only if something states the charge. No reader does: isotope spacing would have to be read off each feature, which is annotation, not conversion. A column full of 1s would claim per-feature knowledge the converter does not have; one scalar in uns claims only what is true.
  • One column per charge (ccs_z1, ccs_z2). Doubles the column for a case MALDI rarely has, and still leaves the consumer to pick.
  • Compute through the vendor library on TDF and the formula elsewhere. Two routes, two sets of values for the same pairs, and a store that depends on the machine. Rejected for the reasons above.
  • A drift-time CCS. Needs the cell length, field, pressure and temperature, or single-field calibrants. No source Thyra reads states them, and Waters drift-time data is not read at all.

Cost. 8 bytes per feature in var, and in the projection D4 makes before building a grid table (VAR_BYTES_PER_FEATURE is 338 now). The values are computed in chunks of about one million features, so the formula's temporaries stay a few MB. On a synthetic 8-million-feature grid the peak of building and wrapping var rose by at most 8 bytes per feature. D8 stands: var is still the memory peak.

What changes in a store. Every mobility table on a 1/K0 axis gains var["ccs"] and uns["ccs"], and the schema version in every table's msi_metadata is 0.13.0. Every other array is unchanged. Stores written earlier are unchanged and still valid. thyra validate checks that a ccs column, on whatever table carries it, is numeric, finite, positive and as long as mz.

Known limits.

  • The value is for charge 1. A multiply charged feature's stored CCS is wrong, and the store cannot tell which features those are.
  • On a grid table the pair is the mass bin and the channel centre, so the value is that cell's, not one peak's. The 1/K0 it rests on can be up to half a channel from a peak's own.
  • A 1/K0 array that states no unit gets no column. If real TIMSCONVERT or TIMSImaging exports turn out to omit the unit, this gate is the place to relax.
  • Processed imzML with a mobility array keeps no mobility table, so no CCS.

docs.title: D48. A store in micrometres places its raster where the source did
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-14). Amended by D69 (2026-10-19): an optical image with no alignment is not in "global" at all.

Decision. A store whose "global" is in micrometres gets one more coordinate system, "acquisition". Every TIC image, pixel polygon element and optical image placed in micrometres carries a transform to it: the element's "global" transform followed by a Translation to the source's origin. The root attribute coordinate_systems gains an "acquisition" entry beside "global", with origin_um, origin_source and raster_to_acquisition_affine. "global" and the per-dataset system do not change.

The origin is where grid position 0 sits in the source's own frame:

  • Bruker timsTOF, rapifleX, solariX, imzML, mzPeak: the index the source's own numbering gives grid position 0, times the pitch of each axis (D12). origin_source is "raster_index". That index is what the reader records as coordinate_offsets_px: the declared imaging area's or the selected region's minimum (timsTOF), the smallest raster index (solariX), the base the file numbers from, 1 or 0 (imzML, D14, so a cropped file keeps its own coordinates), the .dat header's first raster position (rapifleX, whose indices are already 0-based), or that base plus the writer's position_offset (mzPeak, D29).
  • PHI: 0, which it states.
  • Waters: the fitted lattice origin, the smallest stage reading on each axis, in micrometres. origin_source is "stage_position". It is new: Waters stored no origin before. It reaches the converter as EssentialMetadata.stage_origin_um, because it is not an integer index and cannot go into coordinate_offsets.

On a volume the TIC volume also moves in z, by the z offset times the slice pitch. Pixel polygons stay flat, as they are in "global".

Why. Readers re-zero the raster. Before this, the subtracted offset survived only as two root attributes, coordinate_offsets_px and stage_offset_um, and no element transform carried it. Two stores cut from one slide, such as two --region runs of one .d, landed on top of each other in every SpatialData reader. Placing them took Thyra-specific code. Now any reader that follows transforms places them.

The name. "acquisition", not "stage": on every format but Waters the origin is a raster index times the pitch, a position in the source's own grid, not a measured stage position. "raster" was rejected because it reads as pixel indices.

When it is not written.

  • A store placed in a FlexImaging scan's pixels (D31). There "global" is already the scan's frame, and the alignment affine absorbs the offset.
  • A source that reports no origin, such as a Waters grid without a fitted lattice. A zero translation would claim an origin nobody stated.
  • An optical image with no alignment. It sits at Identity in "global", which says nothing about where it lies relative to the raster, so moving it by the raster's origin would place it falsely.

What stage_offset_um means now. It was defined as coordinate_offsets_px times the pixel size (D12, D32). It is now "where grid position 0 sits in the source's frame", the same numbers as acquisition.origin_um. For every format that has index offsets the value is unchanged. Waters stores gain it.

Objection that did not win. "Bump convention_version; the attribute has a new top-level key." The key is additive, like z_spacing_um and raster_to_global_affine before it. A consumer that reads only "global" is unaffected, and a bump would make every existing consumer warn on every store.

Reserved name. A dataset_id of "acquisition" is refused, at the front door and by the converter. The per-dataset system is named by the id, so it would silently become this one. "global" stays allowed: both systems would carry the same transform.

What changes in a store. Every micrometre store whose source states an origin gains the "acquisition" transform on its TIC image, pixel polygons and placed optical images, and the coordinate_systems.acquisition entry. Waters stores also gain stage_offset_um, and their raw metadata gains imaging_grid.stage_origin_um. FlexImaging-aligned stores do not change. The metadata schema moves to 0.14.0, which reserves the coordinate system name, as 0.10.0 reserved an obs column (D26). The document's fields do not change. Tables carry no transform, so obs["spatial_x"] and obs["spatial_y"] stay in "global".

Known limits.

  • imzML and mzPeak number from 1 (D14), so most of their stores have an origin one pitch from 0. Two files exported from parts of one acquisition line up only if the exporter kept the acquisition's own numbering.
  • A user-supplied --pixel-size scales an index offset like any other pitch. On Waters it does not move the stage origin, which is measured.
  • A volume's z origin uses the slice pitch. When that pitch is assumed_isotropic, the z origin is as unreliable as the depth.

docs.title: D49. A release is a pull request, and main requires passing checks
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-14), #474. Supersedes D18. The first release pull request, #478, opened on the merge and ran its checks; the required-checks ruleset and auto-merge were turned on after it.

Decision. release-please replaces python-semantic-release. After every merge it keeps one release pull request open, chore(main): release X.Y.Z, which bumps pyproject.toml, thyra/__init__.py, the thyra entry in uv.lock and CHANGELOG.md. Merging that pull request is the release: release-please tags the merge commit and creates the GitHub Release, then release.yml builds the tag and publishes it to PyPI once Tests has passed on that commit. A Monday cron merges the release pull request when Tests passed on it, so releases still come weekly without anyone acting. main gets a ruleset requiring the CI checks, not strict, with no bypass list, and the repository allows auto-merge.

Why. D18 measured that a GITHUB_TOKEN push of the version commit cannot pass a required-checks rule, and that the GitHub Actions app cannot be a bypass actor. Both routes it left open needed a new credential. This removes the push instead: the version commit reaches main through a pull request, like any other change, so the rule needs no bypass and no credential exists to store or rotate. It is the setup Ousia already runs.

The alternative, and why not. A GitHub App holding Contents write, on the ruleset's bypass list, with release.yml pushing as the App. It keeps semantic-release, but adds a private key to store, and checked against python-semantic-release 10.6.1 it is not the one-line change it looks like: remote_settings.token puts GITHUB_TOKEN into the push URL, so the checkout token alone does not change who pushes. Making the App the pusher everywhere would let its GitHub Release start a second release: published run.

What GITHUB_TOKEN costs, and how each is handled (all in release-please.yml):

  • Runs on a pull request it pushed are parked for approval and report no checks. The workflow approves them (.github/scripts/approve-parked-runs.sh).
  • A tag it creates starts no workflow. The workflow dispatches release.yml at the tag.
  • A merge it makes, on the cron path, starts no push run. The workflow runs release-please again in the same job and dispatches Tests at the tag, which the publish gate waits for.

What changes for releases.

  • The Monday cron no longer releases by itself; it merges the release pull request if Tests passed on it. Checks still running defer the release to a dispatch (gh workflow run release-please.yml -f merge_release_pr=true) or the next Monday.
  • The changelog lists feat, fix and perf commits only. Under semantic-release it also listed docs, refactor, test, build and style. release-please releases whenever a visible section is non-empty, so those types are hidden to keep them from triggering a release.
  • New changelog sections use release-please's format. Older ones stay.
  • release.yml runs only on a dispatch at a vX.Y.Z tag and refuses any other ref. Re-publishing a tag is gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z. The publish_only input and the release: published trigger are gone.
  • The PR title check reads its allowed types from release-please-config.json.
  • python-semantic-release left the dev group, and with it ten packages that only it needed.

The ruleset. Required: lint, test and integration on Ubuntu and Windows for Python 3.12 to 3.14, clean-venv-install for 3.12 to 3.14, and Conventional commit title. Not required: Build the site (strict), because docs-check.yml is path-filtered and a code-only pull request would wait for it forever; and complexity-check, which is advisory.

docs.title: D50. A bin wider than the source sampling is rebinned, not sampled
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-13), issue #442.

Decision. tic_preserving checks each spectrum for a sample that interpolation at the bin centres would skip: a bin holding a sample with intensity that is neither of the two samples around its centre. That is three samples in one bin, or two on the same side of its centre; a sample exactly on the centre is read alone, so any other in its bin counts. A skipped zero loses nothing and does not count, so a repeated explicit zero leaves a spectrum alone; two samples at one m/z count when either has intensity, because interpolation reads only one of them.

  • A spectrum with no such bin is resampled exactly as before.
  • A spectrum with one is rebinned wherever a bin holds two or more samples. Each sample stands for its cell, the stretch of m/z from the midpoint with the sample before it to the midpoint with the sample after it. Every bin takes the share of each cell it overlaps. Where the spacing jumps by more than a factor of two, at the edge of a gap, the cell side facing the gap is cut back to the width of the other side.
  • The spectrum's other bins are still interpolated at their centres, then scaled by their width over the spacing of the two samples around the centre, so both kinds of bin hold ion current.

The rescale to the preserved TIC then runs as before. The gap tolerance applies only to interpolated bins: a rebinned bin holds samples and is measured.

The defect this replaces. The operator evaluated the linear interpolant at each bin centre and rescaled the result to the TIC. Once bins are wider than the source spacing that is sampling, not binning. A peak narrower than a bin that falls between two centres is mostly lost, and the rescale hands its ion current to whatever the centres land on. The TIC still balances, so nothing downstream can see it. A spectrum sampled every 0.01 Da with two peaks of 0.05 Da FWHM, onto 0.73 Da bins, against every sample summed into its nearest bin:

total within 1 Da of 167.05 within 1 Da of 333.10 samples summed into bins 56,886.4 20,788 6,536 before 56,886.4 421 415 after 56,886.4 20,788 6,536

On imzml_processed_profile_a (2,965 pixels, sampled every 0.011 Da) onto a constant axis of 2,600 bins (0.731 Da), the mean spectrum against every source spectrum summed into the same bins:

Pearson r rel. L1 sum ratio before 0.132 1.47 1.000 after 1.000 0.057 1.000 after, without the gap cut 1.000 0.076 1.000

The file is processed and has gaps without an explicit zero at their edges, which is what the gap cut is for.

Why this rule. Synthetic profiles were built whose samples are the integral of a known peak shape over each sample's cell, so the ion current each bin should hold is known exactly. Error is rel. L1 against that. The sqrt rows are a zero-suppressed trace on a sqrt(m/z) grid onto linear_tof bins, like the Waters profile route; the constant rows are a constant grid onto constant bins, like rapifleX.

bins per sample before after rebin every bin holding two 0.2 (constant) 0.2768 0.2768 0.2768 1.08 (sqrt) 0.0244 0.0244 0.0245 1.32 (sqrt) 0.0188 0.0188 0.0202 1.40 (constant) 0.0920 0.0920 0.0943 1.90 (sqrt) 0.0210 0.0254 0.0254 2.01 (constant) 0.0778 0.0925 0.0925 2.32 (sqrt) 0.0464 0.0253 0.0253 2.49 (constant) 0.1773 0.0707 0.0707 3.31 (sqrt) 0.1226 0.0198 0.0198 4.14 (sqrt) 0.1939 0.0163 0.0163 8.02 (constant) 0.7637 0.0128 0.0128 29.3 (constant) 1.7784 0.0029 0.0029

Sampling at the centres is as good or better while no sample is skipped, which on an even grid holds below two bins per sample. Past that it falls apart. Rebinning every bin that holds two samples, whatever the spectrum, was measured too (last column): it changes spectra that lose nothing, and costs up to 0.0023 there. Rebinning only the bins that skip a sample was worse between two and three bins per sample (0.1315 against 0.0707 at 2.49): the interpolated bins beside them then hold the wrong share. Once a spectrum is rebinned at all, every bin holding two samples is.

Why cells and not trapezoids. Spreading the trapezoid between each pair of neighbouring samples over the bins it overlaps was measured too. In a separate run, rebinning every bin that holds a sample, it was worse at every width above 1 bin per sample (0.0229 against 0.0161 at 4.14). It also smears a sample over its neighbours' bins even when the axis is the source grid; cells reproduce the source exactly there.

What changes in a store.

  • Conversions whose bins are wide enough to skip samples. For example --resample-method tic_preserving with a coarse --resample-bins or --resample-width-at-mz, the method forced onto the default width for a source sampled more finely than half of it, or a plan_mass_axis plan wider than a source's own width (D43). Their values change, and narrow peaks come back.
  • Not the Waters profile route, the default for a SELECT SERIES MRT and what --waters-spectrum profile takes elsewhere. Its bins are 1.14 times the sample spacing: some hold two samples, one either side of the centre, and none skips one. Measured on waters_desi_profile_a with --waters-spectrum profile (2,436 pixels, 210,636 bins, about 50,000 samples per spectrum): 0 of 87,507,157 stored values changed. The MRT reference run was not on hand; it shares the ratio and the sqrt(m/z) grid, and a synthetic zero-suppressed MRT trace at 1.14 bins per sample is unchanged bit for bit (test_tic_preserving_wide_bins.py).
  • Not the default rapifleX and Bruker MALDI-TOF route. The source is sampled every 24.9 mDa onto a 5 mDa axis, so no bin holds two samples.
  • Not nearest_neighbor, nor any sibling table: they never use this method.

Cost. Deciding that a spectrum skips nothing takes one pass over its sample spacings, against a bound on the bin widths laid once per axis and read once per 64 samples. On a real waters_desi_profile_a spectrum of 46,490 samples that is 0.18 ms of a 2.75 ms resample, and 0.08 ms of 0.80 ms on a 15,000-sample MRT-like trace onto a 1.05M-bin axis. A spectrum that is rebinned costs a few milliseconds more.

Objection: the rule depends on the data (D15). D15 refused an automatic gap tolerance because the stored numbers would depend on a heuristic no flag records. This rule has no setting to record. Whether a centre skips a sample is a fact of the axis and the source, the same in every run. The method name and the Thyra version in the processing step say which operator ran.

Known limits.

  • Between about 1.9 and 2 bins per sample, rebinning is slightly less accurate than sampling (0.0254 against 0.0210; 0.0925 against 0.0778). On an uneven grid a few bins there already skip a sample, and the spectrum is rebinned.
  • A spectrum that is not rebinned keeps the old operator, with its known error when the source and target spacing laws differ (_gate_tic_preserving).
  • The gap cut uses a fixed factor of two. A source whose spacing changes by more than that between neighbouring samples without a gap would have its cells trimmed.

docs.title: D51. A mass axis plan moves an imzML header range out by the precision its text states
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-14).

Decision. When plan_mass_axis takes a range from an imzML source, it moves each header bound out by one unit of the last digit its text states: 100.123457 by 1e-6, 1000 by 1, 1.2E3 by 100. When two texts give the same extreme, the coarser step is used. A low bound that would reach 0 or below is halved instead. This supersedes D43's range rule for imzML sources only; the intersection, the forced bounds and every other format are as D43 describes. A bound the caller forces is used exactly as given. The plan's origins for a derived bound say that an imzML range is its header text moved out.

Why. An imzML header states the lowest and highest observed m/z (MS:1000528 and MS:1000527) as rounded text. The rounded low bound can sit above the source's first sample, and the rounded high bound below its last. A conversion keeps the m/z inside its declared bounds, inclusive, so a plan built from the header as it stands dropped those samples in every spectrum and reported nothing. Measured: on imzml_continuous_profile_a a one-source plan lost one sample per spectrum (620 of 3.4e7 counts); with the step, the planned and unplanned stores both hold 34,446,401.7. A synthetic file lost 15%. The step is read from the text, not the parsed number: 1000 and 1000.000000 parse to the same float, but only the first can hide a sample at 1000.4. A fixed relative margin (1 ppm was tried first) covers six-decimal headers and misses coarser ones. The same file converted without a plan reads the exact extremes of the decoded data and loses nothing.

What changes in a store. A planned conversion of imzML sources lays an axis up to one stated digit wider at a header-derived end and keeps its edge samples; the extra bins are zero in every store. Stores converted without a plan do not change. Nothing released changes: plans are new since 4.4.0.

Known limits.

  • The step bounds rounding and truncation of the stated text. A header whose value is wrong by more than that still cuts samples; the plan cannot tell without decoding spectra.
  • Only imzML sources are moved. Every other format's plan range comes from the same values its conversion uses, so a plan cuts nothing the conversion keeps.

docs.title: D52. The mobility and MS/MS tables keep the m/z range the summed table keeps
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-14). Amended by D82 (2026-10-22).

Decision. The mass-mobility heatmap, the mobility grid table and the demultiplexed MS/MS table keep a point when its m/z is inside the range the summed table keeps (D13): the declared range on a resampled axis, which reaches up to half a bin past the first and last bin centre. A point there goes to the edge bin, as it does in the summed table. A point beyond the range is still dropped. This extends D13 to every table built from the raw points, and lifts the known limit D46 records for its grid and heatmap.

Why. These tables map their points onto the common mass axis with the summed table's nearest-bin rule, but they tested membership against the strict span [axis[0], axis[-1]], the rule D13 retired for the summed table. On a resampled axis whose end centres sit inside the data, the lowest and highest m/z samples of a file were dropped from them while the summed table kept them. Measured on the mobility_processed.imzML fixture with the command line's default resampling and --mobility-grid: the grid table held 810 of the summed table's 1000 counts (current_ratio 0.81, 0.6 in the worst pixel), and the heatmap the same 0.81. Both are now 1.0, with every pixel at 1.0. The same file under --no-resample was already 1.0.

What changes in a store. On a resampled axis that is not constant, points in the half-bin margin at either end now appear in the edge bins of the heatmap counts, the grid table's X and var, and the MS/MS table's X and var. mobility_heatmap.current_ratio, mobility_marginal.current_ratio (with its pixel minimum and maximum) and the MS/MS table's demultiplexed_current ratios move towards 1. Under --no-resample and on a constant axis the kept range is the axis span, so nothing changes. A continuous imzML's shared-axis mobility table drops nothing by m/z and does not change. Released stores: the per-pixel imzML grid is new since 4.4.0 (D46); Bruker TDF heatmaps, grid tables and MS/MS tables change only where a point falls in that margin.

Known limits.

  • The heatmap's stored mz_edges are unchanged. On an axis whose bins widen with m/z the declared upper bound sits a fraction of a bin above the last stored edge, so a point there is counted in the last row while lying just outside the edges that row states.
  • Under tic_preserving the grid's marginal still differs cell by cell from the summed table, as D46 says; only the points each keeps now agree.

docs.title: D53. Waters drift time is read as a mobility axis, and a short list of bins is its own channel set
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-14).

Decision. Two parts.

  1. A Waters function acquired with ion mobility on is converted. Its spectrum is the one MassLynx reports summed over the drift bins, and the bins become the reader's mobility dimension, as a TIMS frame's scans are: uns["mobility_axis"] (drift time, MS:1002476, in ms, UO:0000028; values the drift time of each bin; source "waters_raw"; bin_width the step), uns["mobility_heatmap"], the {table}_mobility sibling with --mobility-grid, and msi_metadata.ms_analysis.ion_mobility. Each bin is read raw (getRawMobilityScanDataPoints), whatever representation the summed table was read in.
  2. When a mobility axis declares itself a list of equal-width bins (MobilityAxis.bin_width) with fewer bins than the 256-channel anchor, the heatmap and the default grid use one channel per bin, edges half a bin outside the first and last value. Every other axis keeps 256 channels over its values. --mobility-bins now defaults to "not given", so --mobility-bins 256 is a choice that keeps 256.

Why part 1. Before it, the reader kept MS functions only, and a mobility function is classified IMS_MS. So every Waters image recorded with mobility on was refused with "No MS functions found": not the drift dimension dropped, the whole image. Measured on an in-house Synapt G2-Si tissue image. The bundled MLReader already exports the calls, which mzmine binds the same way: getNumberOfMobilityScans, getMobility, getRawMobilityScanDataPoints.

Measured on the public MassIVE MSV000092638 Synapt XS image (8,475 scans, MS1) and on in-house Synapt G2-Si runs:

  • 200 bins on every run, equal steps from exactly 0 ms (0.045 to 0.216 ms per bin across runs; 0.06625 ms on the XS image). The step matches the run's "ADC Pusher Frequency" in _extern.inf.
  • driftScanCount on every scan equals the function's bin count.
  • Summed over the bins, the raw points reproduce the profile spectrum's ion current exactly (ratio 1.0 on every sampled scan). The per-bin centroided call is about ten times slower and does not sum to the centroided spectrum (up to 15.6 % off), so it is not bound.

The guard. Over 91 Synapt runs with mobility on, read one per child process: the 56 that declare Acquisition Algorithm: ADC Mode read cleanly; the 35 that do not, all older Synapt G1 runs, crashed the library with an access violation (32) or returned bins that do not sum to the spectrum (3). Even the summed-spectrum read crashed on most of them. An access violation ends the Python process with no message, so on such a run the reader leaves the mobility functions out, decided from the side file before it reads any spectrum, and refuses the run when nothing else is left. That is no regression: before drift time was read, mobility functions were never converted, so those runs store what they stored before, and a run with nothing else was refused then too, as "No MS functions found". getMobility past the last bin raises a C++ exception inside the library, so it is never asked past getNumberOfMobilityScans.

Why part 2. 256 channels over 200 values leave 56 channels holding no value at all, in a fixed comb (1111011101111...): a striped heatmap and 56 empty mobility columns per m/z bin in a grid table. The anchor exists so a heatmap box indexes grid channels. One channel per bin keeps that, because the heatmap and the grid take their channels from the same function (default_channel_plan), and it puts each bin in exactly one channel. The channels are still equal-width, so the grid's law stays "linear". No schema change.

Why a declaration, not a test on the values. "Equal steps, fewer than 256" also describes stubs in the TIMS tests and a synthetic TDF fixture. A real TIMS ramp has 400 to 1,000 scans on a non-linear 1/K0 law. Only the reader knows whether its values are bins it defines or samples of a continuum, so only the Waters reader sets bin_width.

What changes in a store.

  • Waters runs with mobility on, which were refused, now convert. They gain uns["mobility_axis"], uns["mobility_heatmap"] (200 mobility channels) and ion_mobility in the versioned block.
  • uns["mobility_axis"] gains the key bin_width where a reader sets one (Waters only).
  • Waters runs without mobility, and every Bruker and imzML store, are unchanged: their axes declare no bins, so the plan is the 256 anchor it always was.
  • The heatmap is on by default, so a Waters mobility run costs one extra read of every bin: 200 library calls per scan, about 40 ms per scan on the XS image. --no-mobility-heatmap skips it. A grid table costs two more passes; Waters has no single-read frame record as TDF has (D5).

Objections that did not win.

  • "Centroid each bin to match the centroided table." It is ten times slower, it crashed on G1 runs, and centroids of bins still do not sum to the centroid of the sum. The store records the gap instead (current_ratio, with a warning naming --waters-spectrum profile), as it does for TDF vendor_centroid (D1).
  • "Keep 256 everywhere; consumers may assume it." The docs said k = 256. A consumer that hard-codes 256 instead of reading mobility_edges breaks on Waters stores. That is the consumer's fix (the format comes first), and the docs now say to read k.
  • "Probe each file in a child process instead of reading _extern.inf." It would catch crashes the field does not predict, at a process start per conversion. The field separated all 91 runs; a probe can be added if a counter-example appears.

Known limits.

  • getMobility takes no function. The reader refuses mobility when two mobility functions report different bin counts. A run whose functions share a count but not a pusher period would be described by one axis; none has been seen.
  • Functions with and without drift bins on the same pixels (a parallel acquisition): the ones without are converted, as before drift time was read, and the mobility functions are listed under excluded_functions. Functions with and without drift bins on different pixels (chunks of one raster) are all converted, and no mobility is recorded, since the bins would not cover the image. No measured run has either layout.
  • Drift time is not converted to CCS. That needs the run's calibration (getDriftTime_CCS in MassLynxRaw), which is not bound.
  • No public DESI or cyclic IMS image with its .raw folder was found, so neither is tested.

docs.title: D54. pyright checks types in the lint lane, next to mypy
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-15), issue #434.

Decision. The lint job runs pyright 1.1.414 in standard mode as a pre-commit hook, beside mypy. Its settings are [tool.pyright] in pyproject.toml: thyra/ minus the generated ontology tables, Python 3.12, platform Windows, and the project's .venv for third-party types. A pyright error fails lint, so by D19 it can veto a release. To give pyright those types, the job now installs the project's runtime dependencies (not the project itself) as well as the dev group.

Why add it. As configured here, mypy sees less than it appears to. The hook runs it with --ignore-missing-imports and --no-strict-optional, and [tool.mypy] makes pyimzml, spatialdata, anndata, zarr, dask and pandas Any. On 08f0ea4, with the mypy hook green, pyright in standard mode reported 276 errors. A triage found no reachable bug among them, but some were real defects:

  • @register_reader returned an unannotated class, so every reader class read as the base class and its own attributes went unchecked (#483).
  • Untyped abstract copies in the Bruker base reader hid twelve override mismatches (#484).
  • zarr nodes were used as groups unchecked; a malformed store crashed with an unrelated AttributeError or IndexError (#485).
  • A closed or metadata-only timsTOF reader failed on None with an AttributeError that named neither cause (#489).

By the release of 4.5.0 (7845456) the count was 279. #483 to #490 took it to 0 on cb060e8. The gate keeps it there.

Why mypy stays. The two overlap but do not nest. mypy's settings here report what pyright's standard mode does not: unused # type: ignore comments (warn_unused_ignores), unreachable code (warn_unreachable), returning Any from a typed function (warn_return_any) and comparisons that can never be equal (strict_equality). Dropping either checker drops checks the other does not make. Running both costs about ten seconds of pyright per lint run.

What would retire mypy. pyright's own switches for those checks (reportUnnecessaryTypeIgnoreComment and its reachability and Any reporting, or strict mode) turned on and at 0 errors, then mypy's hook removed in a new D-entry. Not before: the lint job would quietly lose checks.

The platform pin. pythonPlatform = "Windows", for the reason [tool.mypy] platform = "win32" exists. Measured on the same tree, Linux and Darwin each report four errors, all of them winreg attributes and ctypes.windll, which exist only on Windows, behind guards that are correct on every platform. Without the pin the verdict depends on the runner.

How the hook is wired. Two settings are load-bearing, and a test guards both:

  • pass_filenames: false. Given file names, pyright checks exactly those and ignores include, so --all-files would hand it tests and scripts. types_or adds toml, so an edit to pyproject.toml alone runs it too.
  • No args. Settings live in pyproject.toml, so the hook and a bare pyright run agree, as flake8's do with .flake8.

Alternatives.

  • "Replace mypy now." It drops the four checks above.
  • "Run pyright as its own CI step, not a hook." That is a second command to keep in step with what a contributor runs locally. D19 chose one command, pre-commit run --all-files, for exactly that reason.
  • "Basic mode." Fewer checks for no gain: standard is pyright's default, and it is the mode the 279 errors were counted and fixed in.

Costs, accepted.

  • The lint job installs spatialdata, dask, zarr and the rest of the runtime tree. It is a larger install than --only-group dev was.
  • A local run needs uv sync first. Without .venv the hook fails on every third-party import. A bare pyright instead uses whatever python is on PATH, so its verdict then depends on the machine.
  • The hook env downloads the pyright package from npm when it is built. Like D19's GitHub dependency, an outage there can turn lint red.
  • The rev is not in uv.lock, so nothing moves it; bump it by hand, re-measure, and fix what a newer pyright reports in the same PR.

docs.title: D55. Non-finite values decide nothing, and a mislabelled polarity term is read on spectra
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-16). Amends D34 and D35.

Decision. Four rules, each about a value that is not what it claims to be.

  • The intensity threshold sums measurements only. A point whose m/z is not finite, or whose intensity is not finite or is negative, is in no peak's sum. Its own mask entry stays true: the converter drops, counts or refuses it exactly as it does with no threshold set. Every reader and both mobility passes call the one helper, summed_peak_mask. The timsTOF mobility and window tables test summed digitizer counts instead, which cannot be NaN or negative. A spectrum of only finite, non-negative values takes the helper's first branch, which is the old body unchanged, so its store is byte-identical.
  • A non-finite m/z is dropped before resampling, by either method. The converter drops it with the unusable intensities and counts it in the same warning, on a resampled axis. nearest_neighbor already dropped it as out of range, but tic_preserving interpolated over it: an infinity gave the spectrum no bins at all, and a NaN made every bin NaN. On the raw axis it is var["mz"] itself, and the axis check refuses it.
  • The imzML source range is taken over finite m/z. A spectrum's NaN or infinite m/z adds nothing to it, and a resolved range that is still not finite (an API bound of inf, or another reader's range) is refused in one line, as an empty range is.
  • MS:1000128 named "positive scan" states positive polarity on a spectrum too. pyimzml already corrects that pair to MS:1000130 in fileContent and the parameter groups. Thyra applies the same correction to the per-spectrum terms, and to the first spectrum on the metadata-only route. The name decides it, so a true "profile spectrum" term is untouched. The spectrum-type fallback no longer reads the mislabelled term as profile.

Why. The converter drops a NaN, infinite or negative intensity before resampling (_drop_unusable_intensities), but the threshold summed raw values first. So one unusable copy of a peak decided it. A NaN copy removed a peak of 100 that the store kept without a threshold; an infinite copy kept a peak whose only usable share was 10, under a threshold of 50. The grouping also put an infinite m/z into the largest finite peak, because the split test step > 1e-12 * m/z is false for infinity.

The source range took the minimum and maximum of every value. One infinite m/z made it infinite, and the default conversion ended in OverflowError: cannot convert float infinity to integer. A NaN made its spectrum's extrema NaN, which the running minimum then skipped, finite peaks included, so the range could come out narrower than the data.

The polarity term was matched by accession alone on a spectrum. A file that stated the mislabelled pair on every spectrum stored no polarity, while the same pair in a group gave "positive". The same statement should give the same value wherever the file puts it.

What changes in a store.

  • Stores converted with --intensity-threshold from sources whose repeated m/z carry a NaN, infinite or negative intensity, or that hold an infinite m/z: they keep or drop different peaks. Stores of sources with only finite, non-negative values do not change.
  • --no-resample with --intensity-threshold on a source with a NaN m/z is now refused, as it is without a threshold. Before, the threshold dropped the NaN point whenever that point's group did not reach the threshold (a NaN sum never does), and the conversion then succeeded.
  • Processed imzML with a NaN m/z: essential_metadata.mass_range, and so the default axis, now covers every finite peak. Such a file converted on main too, on a range that could miss the spectra holding a NaN. Files with an infinite m/z, and continuous files with a non-finite shared m/z, now convert by default instead of failing. With --no-resample they are still refused, since those values would become var["mz"].
  • Resampled with tic_preserving (the default for some profile sources), a spectrum with a non-finite m/z keeps its finite peaks, where an infinity stored it empty and a NaN stored it as NaN.
  • imzML files that state "positive scan" under MS:1000128 on each spectrum gain polarity and polarity_term (as MS:1000130), and the root acquisition_parameters polarity. When fileContent states no spectrum type, such a file is no longer stored as profile.

No schema change: every field already exists.

Known limits.

  • An mzPeak archive of a Bruker run sums raw counts per TDF-scale bin (_on_tdf_scale) before the threshold helper runs, so a NaN count still reaches that bin's sum there, and an infinite m/z still joins the largest finite bin. "Every reader calls the one helper" holds for the threshold test, not for that earlier grouping. PR #514 fixes it.
  • When the threshold removes every measurement and only unusable points reach the converter, the empty-store refusal blames the unusable values and does not name the threshold.

Costs, accepted. The term correction runs one more XML lookup on each spectrum that states no correct polarity term itself. Measured on a 60,000 spectrum file with the polarity in a group: parse 3.20 s to 3.58 s (median of five). The hook is pyimzml's private per-spectrum step; a test converts a file that states the pair on each spectrum, so a pyimzml release that renames the step fails there.

Alternatives.

  • "Drop unusable points in the threshold's mask." Then --no-resample with a threshold would silently drop an infinite m/z that it refuses without one. Leaving them to the converter keeps one rule for them.
  • "Refuse a source with any non-finite m/z." A resampled axis has no use for those values, and dropping them as out of range is what happens to any peak outside the axis.
  • "Add MS:1000128 to the polarity accessions." Every "profile spectrum" term would then read as positive.

docs.title: D56. The resampling step records the axis it describes, and refusals name the way forward
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-16). Amends D43.

Decision. Four rules, so that what a conversion says matches what it did.

  • bins_per_fwhm is honoured or refused. It is refused beside width_at_mz or target_bins, which each fix the bin count of a tof axis too, and on an axis that resolves to any other type. These are the rules plan_mass_axis already applied. The option exists only in the Python API.
  • The step records the width the axis has. When a width set the bin count, mass_width_da is that width, as before. When target_bins set it, or the floor of 100 bins raised it, mass_width_da is the bin width at reference_mz that the count gives, and on a tof axis so is bins_per_fwhm. A width law (tof_a, tof_b, bins_per_fwhm) is recorded on a tof axis only. A plan keeps its width as its setting, and its origins and warnings state the width it lays.
  • An empty range from the source names the way through. When both bounds came from the source and its range is a single m/z, the refusal names --resample-min-mz / --resample-max-mz and, for a source whose peaks all sit at that m/z, --no-resample. A plan of one such source says its range is a single m/z.
  • A Waters range widened past the acquisition range is reported where it sets the axis. The extractor logs the widening at debug. The axis planner warns, and only for a bound the source's range set: typed bounds and a plan give no such warning.

Why. Each case was a statement that did not hold.

  • bins_per_fwhm beside a width was dropped without a word. Beside target_bins it was recorded as applied, though the count fixed the axis. On a constant axis it changed nothing and was still recorded. plan_mass_axis refused the same requests, so a plan and a conversion disagreed on what is allowed.
  • The step took mass_width_da from the request or the default, whatever fixed the axis. A width of 1.0 Da over 500-510 m/z recorded 1 for an axis of 100 points 0.101 Da apart. target_bins 100 on a constant axis over 100-1000 recorded the 5 mDa default for points 9.09 Da apart.
  • A source whose every peak sat at m/z 500 was refused as "[500, 500] is empty" with no remedy. --no-resample and typed bounds both convert it.
  • The Waters extractor warned that "the resampled axis is widened" while it read the metadata, before typed bounds or a plan applied. With --resample-min-mz 700 --resample-max-mz 900 the axis was 700-900 and the next warning said those peaks were dropped.

Why the recorded width is the count's in two cases only. Every generator lays its bins from the range and the count alone, so the count fixes the width. When a width set the count on a physics axis, the width the axis has differs from it only by the truncation to a whole number of bins. Recording the request there keeps every other store unchanged. Where the count came from elsewhere, the request says nothing about the axis.

A constant axis is the exception. A width w sets n = (max - min) / w, but the generator lays n points, so the step is (max - min) / (n - 1), wider by n / (n - 1). At the 5 mDa default over 900 Da that is about 6 parts in a million; at the 100-bin floor it is 1%. The step records the request there as before, so the same constant axis records w when a width laid it and the laid step when a count or the floor did. Recording the laid step always would change every constant store's step for a difference no reader acts on. Whether the floor applied is read from the count the width lays, never by comparing widths, since the laid step can come out wider than the width asked for.

Why refuse bins_per_fwhm off a tof axis, when --tof-law only warns. bins_per_fwhm has no CLI flag, and plan_mass_axis already refuses it. --tof-law is a CLI flag whose warning existing commands rely on; that warning stays, and its values are no longer recorded.

What changes in a store. Only the mass axis resampling processing step in msi_metadata, for conversions that used target_bins, a width the floor raised, or a width law on a non-tof axis. The data, var and every other store are unchanged. No schema change: the step's parameters are free-form scalars.

What changes for callers. API calls that set bins_per_fwhm beside width_at_mz or target_bins, or on a non-tof axis, are refused where they were accepted.

Alternatives.

  • "Leave the fields out when the count fixed the axis." The step merges the request under the resolved values, so a left-out field would fall back to the request, the value this fixes.
  • "Always record the width the axis has." Every store's step would change by the truncation, for no reader's benefit.
  • "Warn on bins_per_fwhm off a tof axis, as for --tof-law." A plan would refuse what a conversion accepts.

docs.title: D57. A store keeps its source's regions, and a region store describes only its own
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-16), issue #496. Superseded in part by D83 (2026-10-22): a Waters run with a MultiRegions table in its method file keeps those regions; "Region 1 stays only for ... Waters" now holds only for a Waters run that declares none.

Decision. A store describes the regions it holds, with the numbers and names its source states. Under region=, everything the timsTOF reader reports is about the selected region. Five rules follow.

  • A reader that knows its regions gives a region map and a region summary for one region too: timsTOF (the DB RegionNumber), rapifleX (the poslog's R{n}), mzPeak (the region each scan names, or its one listing) and solariX, which already did. A single-region store then keeps the source's number, name and box instead of the placeholder region 1. This supersedes D44's "As on timsTOF, one region gives no map" and its "A single-region Rapiflex store is unchanged". Region 1 stays only for formats with no region concept (imzML, PHI, Waters). On timsTOF the name of a lone region is the .mis Area the alignment pairs it with, which on a run cut from a multi-region slide is the one its spot names give, while the number stays the database's, the one region= accepts. region= accepts that name too, and refuses another Area's name on such a run.

  • get_region_info, and with it uns["regions"], lists only the selected region. Its count and box are that region's, inside the stored raster.

  • The precursor schedule is read from the selected region's frames: the frame types in Frames, and the windows in PasefFrameMsMsInfo, DiaFrameMsMsInfo and FrameMsMsInfo. The mixed-level check already filtered this way. Without region= the queries are unchanged.
  • A position measured in two regions is one row, as any repeated position is (D40). On timsTOF and solariX that row takes the region of its first frame that holds peaks, the frame whose number is its acquisition_order (D26), and on mzPeak the region of its first scan. An empty frame gives no row, so it names no region. The reader warns once, naming the regions and the first shared position.
  • region takes any integer type except bool, so a value read back from obs["region_number"], which is a numpy integer, selects its region.

uns["average_spectrum_per_region"] is written when the region map holds two regions or more: one region's mean is the table's own average_spectrum. A region with no row has no entry in it, on every reader. D26's note on column types is corrected in place, with a dated note: in a 2D store x, y and region_number are int32, not int64.

Why. A single-region run was stored as region 1 with no name, whatever the source said: a timsTOF run with one region numbered 3, or an mzPeak archive naming region 3 "tumour", came out as region 1, while the optical crop record of the same store named region 0 and Area "01". The placeholder also broke the region loop: list_regions answered 1 for a single-region .d whose region is 0, and region=1 was then refused. Runs of one slide merged on region_number could collide, because the placeholder 1 equals another run's real region 1.

A region= store listed every region of the run, with whole-run counts and boxes outside its raster, some negative. A region on one constant schedule lost its MS/MS table when another region was survey only, because the survey frames of the other region made the file "mixed". A survey region was described as MS level 2. A shared position took the region of its last frame and the order of its first, so one row named two different frames. A region number read back from a store was refused with a message about positional arguments nobody passed. A region with no row got a mean of zeros, which is not a mean.

What changes in a store.

  • A single-region timsTOF store: obs["region_number"] changes from 1 to the DB RegionNumber, which was 0 on all five single-region runs measured (2026-10-16), and the uns["regions"] entry gains bounds and, where the .mis has it, name. The same holds for a single-region rapifleX store (the poslog's number, usually 0) and a single-region mzPeak archive of a Bruker run.
  • A single-region solariX store and a region= timsTOF store lose uns["average_spectrum_per_region"], which held a copy of average_spectrum. A multi-region store keeps it, even when only one of its regions holds rows.
  • A region= timsTOF store: uns["regions"] holds one entry. The fragmentation block and whether an _msms table is written follow the region's own frames.
  • A multi-region timsTOF or solariX store with a shared position: that row's region_number is the region of its first frame (it was the last), and the per-region means move with it.
  • A store with a region that has no row: that region's average_spectrum_per_region entry is gone.

Alternatives.

  • "Write no region map when two regions share a position", as the rapifleX reader does (D44). Rejected for timsTOF and solariX: their region number is a column of the vendor database, so one shared position does not cast doubt on the others. The rapifleX map is rebuilt from spot names, and a conflict there can mean the keying itself is wrong.
  • "Keep each region's spectrum in its own row." The store has one row per position (D40); two rows at one (x, y) would break every consumer that indexes by position. region= gives each region its own measurement.
  • "An all-NaN mean for an empty region." A consumer that plots every entry then draws nothing under a legend label. No entry says the same thing.

Known limits.

  • A consumer that picked a single-region store's rows with region_number == 1 now finds none on timsTOF, rapifleX and mzPeak.
  • On a timsTOF run cut from a multi-region slide (RegionNumber 0, spot names R02...), the optical crop record names region 2 while obs["region_number"] is 0. The name agrees; the alignment's number is not part of this decision.
  • A rapifleX run whose poslog misses a spectrum's spot, and an older mzPeak archive whose one listed box does not hold every pixel, still get the placeholder 1, with a warning, new for a single-region run: before, one region was not checked at all.
  • In the full store, a shared position's row sums the spectra of both regions, so the earlier region's mean is not the one its region= store gives. The warning says so.
  • The schedule filter needs MaldiFrameInfo. A region= request on a file without it is already refused (issue #252).
  • A frame that lists peaks but loses all of them to --intensity-threshold still counts as holding peaks, so on a shared position it can name the region while a later frame gives the row its acquisition_order.

docs.title: D58. The mass-mobility heatmap is a mean over the summed table's rows
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-16), issue #495. Narrows D38's divisor and lifts its first known limit.

Decision. A spectrum the summed table gives no row adds neither points nor a pixel to uns["mobility_heatmap"]. On the fused route (a TDF), a frame feeds the heatmap only when it gets a row. On the separate raw pass (imzML, Waters), the converter tells the heatmap which positions have a row once the passes have decided them. The heatmap's population is then the one uns["average_spectrum"] divides by, as D38 meant it to be.

Three smaller rules come with it:

  • The shared-axis mobility table (a continuous imzML with a mobility array) takes the grid route's memory guard (D4) before it builds anything, on the distinct (m/z, mobility) pairs the list holds, which are its var. Past half of free memory the table is left out with a WARNING naming --no-mobility-table, once per table; past a quarter it warns and is built.
  • A mobility spectrum with no row counts as skipped only when it is on the table's own plane and carries signal, on the separate pass and the fused one alike. Another plane's spectrum has its row in that plane's table, and an all-zero one loses nothing.
  • A 2D conversion of a multi-plane source plans a table for each plane the pre-scan meets, not for every z in the span. A single plane and a volume are planned up front, as before.

Why. On a continuous imzML with one all-zero spectrum, --no-resample or not, the summed table had three rows and the heatmap four pixels: current_ratio 0.75 and a warning, though no current was lost. D38 kept the heatmap's own count of distinct positions and rejected taking the table's rows, because one raw pass served every plane and the fallback has no table. Both still hold, so the rows are not handed over as a number: the heatmap asks, per position, whether the table has a row there. The fallback, with no table, still counts every position.

The other three were seen in the same run. A feature list the grid guard would refuse went through, and could end in a raw allocation error. Each plane of a two-plane conversion warned that the other plane's spectra "had no row ... and were skipped". A source stating z 1 and z 120 planned 120 tables: 118 warnings, and 14.4 s against 4.5 s for the same six spectra on z 1 and 2.

What changes in a store.

  • A store with a mobility heatmap and a spectrum that gets no row (all zero, every point outside the kept mass range, off the grid, or a TDF frame whose vendor centroid is empty while its raw scans are not): counts changes from (all points) / (positions fed) to (points of the spectra with a row) / (rows), and current_ratio with it. On the issue's file, whose rowless spectrum is all zero, that is a factor of 4/3, and current_ratio goes from 0.75 to 1.0.
  • Every store without a rowless spectrum is byte-identical: measured on the eight default fixtures and two TDF runs, before and after.
  • A store whose shared-axis feature list is too wide for the machine has no _mobility table, and uns does not name one.
  • A TDF store under scan_sum, with the default mass range and no intensity threshold, does not change: every frame with raw points then has a summed spectrum, so every one already had a row. A narrowed range or a threshold that empties a frame changes it as the first bullet says.
  • Planning tables per plane met changes no store: the planes the pre-scan never met had no rows, so they wrote no table before either.

Alternatives.

  • "Divide by the table's row count." The separate pass builds every plane's heatmap at once (D41), so it would need every plane's count, and an off-grid spectrum's points would stay in the numerator.
  • "Skip all-zero spectra in the imzML reader." The reader belongs to every route, and a spectrum off the grid or outside the mass range would still be counted. The converter is where rows are decided.
