A folder holding one solariX run now converts, where the solariX reader refused it; its store equals the store of the .d itself. Stores converted from a .d, or from a folder holding one timsTOF run, are unchanged.

Alternatives.

  • "Keep the first run in sorted order, with a warning." A script still gets an unchosen run at exit 0.
  • "Say in the docs that the library takes the first run." The pick stays silent.

docs.title: D79. A store appears under its output name only when it is complete
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22), issue #525. Extends the .failed move of #245 and #293.

Decision. The converter writes its store under a temporary name in the output's folder, <name>.incomplete-<8 hex>. Every step that touches the store targets that name: the write, the optical pixel streaming and the removal of a dropped image, and the metadata consolidation. The store is renamed to the output name as the last step, and marked complete only then. A failure Python sees moves the temporary store to <name>.failed, as before; the converter does this itself, so a caller that builds a converter directly gets it too. A run that is killed leaves only the temporary folder and its .thyra_* scratch, and the same command runs again at once. The rename is retried for two seconds, as Windows now and then refuses one for a moment. If it still fails, the run fails, its error names the temporary folder and says the store in it is complete, and nothing is moved to .failed. The Windows path budget (prepare_zarr_output_path) is measured on the temporary name, which is 20 characters longer. thyra validate on a store with no metadata block names an unfinished write as a possible cause, and names a .incomplete-<hex> folder as the temporary folder of a conversion that did not finish.

Why. An out-of-memory kill, or a native abort in pyarrow or pandas, gives Python no chance to run the move to .failed. The partial store stayed under the output name, the retry was refused because the output existed, and thyra validate blamed an old Thyra version.

What changes in a store. Nothing in its contents. While a conversion runs, its store sits under the temporary name beside the output, and it appears under the output name only once it is complete.

Alternatives.

  • "Keep writing in place and narrow the docs to failures the process survives." The retry after a kill stays blocked.
  • "Mark the store unfinished and let the next run move a marked store aside." The path check gains a rule that moves an existing path.

Known limits. A Ctrl-C that lands between the consolidation and the rename is a failed run: the complete store goes to .failed, because the output name does not hold it yet.

docs.title: D80. Every output file follows the store path's rule
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22), issue #525.

Decision. --log-file, thyra metadata -o, thyra export-metaspace -o (and its default beside the store) and thyra-check-ontology --output go through one helper, thyra/utils/output_files.py, that checks the path before any work starts. A missing folder is created when the file is written, as it is for the store. A path that is an existing folder, or that lies under a regular file, is refused with one line and exit 2. A --log-file at the output store's path, or inside it, is refused too, since writing it would create the output.

Why. Each command opened its file without a check and ended in a traceback, after the metadata read or the ontology check had already run; a --log-file in a new folder stopped the conversion before it started. Creating rather than refusing keeps one rule for every output; the cost is that a typo makes a stray folder, as it already does for the store.

What changes in a store. Nothing.

docs.title: D81. The spectrum type and the instrument follow the spectra that are converted
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22), issue #526. Amends D29 (the instrument, and its chilli known limit); relates to D45.

Decision. What a store records about its spectra is read from the spectra it holds, not from the file's summary or from list order.

  • The spectrum type is the one every converted spectrum states. On imzML a spectrum states it through its own terms and the parameter groups it references; a group no spectrum references counts for nothing. On mzPeak it is the spectrum_representation column of the spectra kept: on a pixel, and not an MSn spectrum left out beside MS1 (D70, D73). An archive read from its peaks member stays centroid, and one that fills both members stays profile, as the member decides. When the converted spectra state both types, no type is recorded and one warning gives the counts; the axis is then chosen as for an unknown type. When the spectra state one type and the file-level declaration (fileContent, file_description.contents) names only the other, the spectra win, with a warning. The declaration counts only when no spectrum states a type, and only if it names exactly one; naming both leaves the type unset. The processed-mode guess runs only when nothing is stated anywhere. --spectrum-type still overrides, and its contradiction warning compares with the type the spectra give. One function applies the rule on both routes.
  • The instrument (model, serial number, analyzer, axis family) comes from the configuration the converted spectra use: on imzML the one each spectrum's first scan names, else the run's default; on mzPeak the scans' instrument_configuration_id, else run.default_instrument_id. A name the list does not hold counts as none, so the default decides for it (the pyimzml writer names one that does not exist). Each configuration is resolved alone. A fact the used configurations state differently is left unset, with a warning; a configuration that states a TOF counts against another's Orbitrap family.
  • A serial number written as a JSON number is kept as text.
  • The solvent (IMS:1001211) on the used configuration or one of its components is written to preparation.solvent. export-metaspace writes an unstated solvent as "" with a warning, not "none": a DESI source sprays one.
  • The z spacing is written to conversion_options only on a volume of more than one plane, as in coordinate_systems. Elsewhere nothing applied it, and the log already said it is not recorded.

Why. The 4.3.3 stress test (#427) found five rules answering one question: the imzML file description (centroid first), the imzML document order (any group, used or not), the mzPeak contents order, the mzPeak column (any one centroid label wins), and both members filled (profile). An imzML and its own archive could be binned on different axes at exit 0, and so could a file with an unused group or a left-out MS2 spectrum. The type picks the axis, so this changed var and X.

Finding Before After F176: unused centroid group, 30 profile spectra centroid, 219,722 bins (group first) profile, 120,000 bins F178: fileContent lists both, spectra profile imzML centroid, archive first-listed profile on both routes, either order F179: 8 profile labels and 1 centroid centroid, 1,988 bins unset with a warning, 999 bins F179: centroid MS2 left out centroid profile, 999 bins F175: two configurations, spectra use rapifleX model of the first listed rapifleX in either order F216: serial as a JSON number dropped '1877407.00228' F72: DESI file states methanol Solvent: "none" Solvent: "methanol" F62: one plane, --handle-3d --z-spacing 5 z_spacing_um: 5 in conversion_options not written

The report measured the public chilli imzML: fileContent declares profile while all 4,166 spectra state centroid. It was stored as profile on 396,849 bins and its archive as centroid on 978,495. Following the spectra gives both the archive's axis, which lifts D29's chilli known limit. Two options lost. Leaving the type unset whenever both are declared would strip the type from files whose spectra all agree. Recording profile would bin an all-centroid file on the profile axis.

What changes. The recorded type and axis of files whose spectra disagree with their summary or with each other; the instrument of files whose spectra do not use the first-listed configuration; preparation on sources that state a solvent; and the two z keys leave conversion_options on every store that is not a multi-plane volume. Every store with one configuration and spectra that agree with fileContent keeps its type, axis and instrument.

Known limits.

  • The metadata-only route (thyra metadata, preview, plan_mass_axis) reads the head and the first spectrum, so it follows the first spectrum's type and configuration. It differs from a conversion only for a file whose later spectra say otherwise, as for polarity (D35).
  • The chilli imzML and the other public example files were not converted for this entry; the before and after above come from the stress report and constructed files.
  • Laser parameters (imzmldict) are still taken from the first configuration that states them, and the polarity rule still reads every parameter group, used or not.
  • No real file with two instrument configurations has been seen. The rule is tested on constructed imzML files and archives.
  • A pyimzml parser a caller builds without Thyra's reader records nothing per spectrum. ImzMLMetadataExtractor over it falls back to fileContent and every configuration, as it does for polarity and MS levels, so it can report another type or instrument than a conversion of the same file.

docs.title: D82. A mobility table holds only mobility measured inside its edges, on a shared axis proven on every spectrum
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22). Amends D34, D46 and D52.

Decision. Five rules about what a mobility-resolved table may hold.

  • A stated mobility range drops what lies outside it. With --mobility-min or --mobility-max, a point beyond the stated range is left out of the grid table and counted in one WARNING. A range that holds no point writes no grid table, and says so. A range read off the values (the default) still clips its overhang into the edge channels, as the heatmap does. This is D13's rule for a stated m/z range, applied to mobility.
  • The shared-axis table keeps the summed table's m/z range. A feature whose m/z lies outside the range the summed table keeps (D52) is left out of var and of every row, and the count is said at WARNING.
  • A shared (m/z, mobility) feature list is proven on every spectrum. An imzML gets one only when every converted spectrum points at one m/z block, measured from the offsets, and every mobility array equals the first, NaN for NaN. A copy at the first one's offset is not re-read, nor is any block twice. Otherwise the file is per-pixel mobility and is converted as the same bytes declared processed are: no shared-axis table, no axis values, and the heatmap over the values (D46); --mobility-grid is the way to a mobility table. The same measured block test decides the extractor's mass range and the reader's common mass axis, so a file that declares continuous mode but writes a block per spectrum is read as processed, with one WARNING. The file's file_mode metadata still records what it declares.
  • A non-finite mobility value withholds the mobility. A NaN or infinite value anywhere in an imzML's converted mobility arrays writes the summed table and no mobility table, heatmap, grid or uns["mobility_axis"]. One WARNING names the file and the count. msi_metadata still records that the file declares a mobility array (ion_mobility.present), which it does.
  • A TDF mzPeak archive's TOF bin is grouped within 1e-7, relative. Its copies of one bin are summed into one point before the intensity threshold, as the .d reader sums them.

When a grid is asked for and not written, the reason is said once: no mobility dimension (a Bruker TSF file, a non-finite value), or --no-mobility-table, naming any sizing option given with it. --tdf-spectrum and the grid options are named as ignored on a TSF file, on the command line and through reader_options.

Why. The 4.3.3 stress test (#427) found each of these at exit 0.

Finding Before After F13: synthetic_tims, --mobility-min 1.0 --mobility-max 1.5 206 points clipped into edge channels, current_ratio 1.0 dropped and counted, current_ratio 0.6417 F13: the same at 3.0 to 4.0 all current in one channel no grid table, with the reason F129: mobility_continuous, m/z 400 to 500 m/z 300 and 600.25 in the edge columns left out; the mz_index marginal equals the summed table F121: continuous declared, a block per spectrum m/z 50 and 2000 dropped row sums 6, 15, 24 on an axis of 50 to 2000 F185: 144 spectra, spectrum 71 differs stored at spectrum 0's mobility per-pixel mobility F186: the same, spectrum 9's own m/z filed under spectrum 0's m/z, or refused with a threshold per-pixel mobility, either way F168: an infinity in the shared axis a store thyra validate rejects summed table only; validates F205: equal copies holding a NaN "differ between spectra" the NaN named and counted

A clipped point lies at a mobility it was never measured at, and the marginal over channels hid it: current_ratio stayed 1.0. The drop makes the ratio say how much the stated range left out.

The 64-spectrum sample was chosen for cost, but nothing recorded the choice, and the property it tests is about every spectrum. The proof reads each mobility block once. Measured on a continuous export of 2,000 spectra by 50,000 features with a copy per spectrum (0.80 GB of mobility, 1.60 GB .ibd, warm page cache): 0.57 s for the proof against 0.01 s for the sample. One pass over the intensities of the same file took 0.22 s, and a conversion reads them at least twice. The file was synthetic: no real TIMS export with a mobility array was at hand.

MS-Numpress stores each scan's row on its own scale, so one TOF bin's copies decode up to the row's largest m/z over 2^31 apart: 7e-8 relative at m/z 20 in a row reaching 3000. TOF bins lie some 1e-6 apart or more (6.06e-6 the closest pair on synthetic_tims). At 1e-12 each scan's copy was tested alone, and a peak whose sum passes the threshold was lost.

What changes in a store.

  • Grid tables converted with --mobility-min or --mobility-max from a source with points beyond them: fewer entries in X, no features in the edge channels from those points, and mobility_marginal.current_ratio below 1.
  • Shared-axis tables under a resampled range narrower than the features: fewer features in var and fewer columns in X.
  • An imzML that declares continuous mode but writes a block per spectrum: every peak kept, on a processed axis; essential_metadata.mass_range covers every spectrum; with a mobility array, no shared-axis table.
  • A continuous imzML whose mobility copies differ only outside the old sample: per-pixel mobility (no shared-axis table).
  • An imzML with a NaN or infinite mobility: no mobility table, heatmap or uns["mobility_axis"]. Before, it got a heatmap and grid without the points that had one (D46), or a store thyra validate rejected.
  • Thresholded TDF mzPeak archives under MS-Numpress keep the peaks their .d keeps. Other archives already summed their bins and do not change.

Stores converted without stated mobility bounds, from finite imzML files whose spectra share one block, and from .d folders, do not change.

Objections considered.

  • Clip on a stated range too, and warn. The table would still hold current at a mobility it was not measured at, and a consumer reads the table, not the log.
  • Refuse a non-finite mobility. The summed table is right and is most of the store. The m/z rule (D55) drops a non-finite m/z and keeps the rest; a mobility value has no table of its own to drop it from, so the mobility products go instead.
  • Keep the sample and warn that it is one. A wrong axis at exit 0 is the failure, and the cost of the proof is one read of the mobility arrays.

Known limits.

  • The .d reader's mobility comes from scan numbers and the Waters reader's from drift bins; neither can be NaN, and neither is checked.
  • A processed-declared file whose spectra all point at one m/z block is still read as processed: the measured test is applied only to a continuous declaration.
  • The metadata-only route (preview_msi) still takes a continuous declaration's range from the first spectra when their recorded extrema agree (issue #371).
  • No MS-Numpress archive from mzpeak-convert 0.16.0 was converted for this entry; the tolerance rests on the encoding's own error bound.

docs.title: D83. A Waters run keeps the regions its method declares, on one grid as on timsTOF
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22). Supersedes in part D44 and D57, and D72's known limit on regions. Amends the one-lattice rule of the Waters raster fit.

Decision. A Waters run whose method file (<run>.xml inside the .raw) holds a MultiRegions table has regions, and the store keeps them the way a timsTOF store does.

  • Numbers. Regions are numbered 1, 2, ... in table order. The table states no number. Starting at 1 keeps region 1 on every Waters store without a table, and on a run whose scans all lie in the first box.
  • Membership. A scan belongs to the declared box (start and length, in mm) that holds it, widened by half the declared step on each side. The widening is needed: a line scan's box is 0.01 mm tall and its step 0.02 mm. If any positioned scan lies in no box or in two, the regions are not used, a warning says why, and the run is read as one raster, as before; region= is then refused. A scan of a later function chunk that lies in no box is off the raster; one in a declared box counts as on it, so a region acquired only in the tail chunk of a split raster is kept.
  • Placement. Each region holding scans gets its own lattice, so the off-raster refusal is tested within one region. All regions sit on one grid at their stage positions. The pitch is the regions' shared fitted pitch, which must agree within 1 %; on an axis no region can measure, it is the declared step. The grid starts at the smallest region origin on each axis. Each region's origin is rounded to the nearest grid line, and format_specific.regions records its stage origin, grid offset and placement_shift_um: how far its stage origin lies from the grid line it was placed on.
  • Summary. obs["region_number"], uns["regions"] (number, scan count, box), uns["average_spectrum_per_region"] and thyra.list_regions follow D57. A declared region with no scan is not listed.
  • Selection. region=N (--region N) converts one declared region alone, and the store describes only that region (D57). A run without a table accepts region=1, the whole run, as list_regions reports it. A run whose declared regions could not be used refuses every region=. Readers now state whether they select regions (selects_regions); the base reader refuses region for every reader that does not.
  • Line scans. An axis with one stage position takes its pixel size from the method's MaldiXStep or MaldiYStep, where declared, instead of asking for --pixel-size. format_specific.pixel_size_source says, per axis, whether the size came from the stage positions or the method step. --pixel-size still overrides. A single-spot run still has no pixel size and is still refused as no image.

thyra/core/region_map.py gains summarize_regions, which builds the region entries from (x, y, region) per scan. The rapifleX reader uses it too; its entries are unchanged.

Why. A lipid-standard run with two 25-pixel line scans, one on each standard's spot, was refused: the two lines sit 10.16 mm apart in y, and the second starts 170 um (8.46 pitches) to the right of the first, so no one lattice holds both. The method file states the two boxes and the steps, so placing the regions needs no guess beyond the rounding of one origin, and that is recorded. The same file states the y step of every line scan, which Thyra asked the user to type.

timsTOF's region selection was kept as is; only its gate moved to the reader. The SQL paths of timsTOF and solariX stay, because they keep the metadata-only preview cheap. The helper serves the readers that build regions from a list of scans.

What changes in a store.

  • The two-line run now converts: 33 x 509 pixels at 20.1 x 20.0 um, 50 of them with spectra. Region 1 is row 508, columns 0-24; region 2 is row 0, columns 8-32, and its stage origin lies +9.2 um (46 % of a pitch) in x from column 8. --region 2 gives a 25 x 1 store of region 2 alone.
  • A Waters line scan with a declared step now converts without --pixel-size; its y pixel size is the method's step (20.0 um on the lipid standards, whose x pitch is 20.1 um).
  • Every Waters store gains format_specific.pixel_size_source, and a run with a method file gains declared_step_x_um and declared_step_y_um in raw_metadata.imaging_grid.
  • A run whose table declares two regions with scans in only one (an HDSIM run) keeps region_number 1; its uns["regions"] entry gains a box, and format_specific.regions holds its placement.
  • Measured against main on a 25 x 25 run without a table and on the HDSIM run: every array is identical, and only the keys above differ.

Alternatives.

  • "Refuse a run whose regions do not share a lattice, and only accept --region." Two conversions for one run, and no store holding both standards.
  • "Pack the regions next to each other." The grid stays small, but one affine no longer places every region (D75), and the stage geometry is lost.
  • "Number the regions from 0, as Bruker does." Bruker numbers are the source's; Waters states none, and 0 would change region 1 on every Waters store with one region.

Known limits.

  • Regions far apart give a large, mostly empty grid: two 1.5 mm regions 7 mm and 43 mm apart would span about 430 x 2230 pixels. Only filled pixels hold spectra.
  • A rounded region can sit up to half a pitch from its true place relative to the others. Within a region nothing moves.
  • Only Cyclic IMS runs carry the method file. No Synapt or Xevo run has been seen with one.

docs.title: D84. Waters m/z can be lock-mass corrected, without writing to the run
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22).

Decision. --waters-lock-mass MZ|off (reader option lock_mass) chooses the lock-mass correction the stored m/z carry.

  • A reference m/z. The Waters library measures the run's lock-mass scans against it, on a throwaway copy of the run. The copy holds every side file and the lock-mass function's .DAT; the other functions' data files are sparse placeholders of the same size. The library writes its factors (lmgt.inf) into the copy, Thyra reads them, and the copy is deleted. Each converted scan's m/z -- the summed spectrum, its drift bins and the shared mass axis -- are multiplied by the factor interpolated linearly at the scan's retention time, held at the first and last measurement outside them.
  • off. The m/z are stored uncorrected.
  • Omitted (the default). The store keeps what the run carries. When the run folder holds an lmgt.inf (a correction MassLynx saved), the library applies it to every read, and it is kept. When it holds none but the run has lock-mass reference scans, a warning says so and names the option.

The library applies an lmgt.inf in the run folder to every read, so a scan's m/z are multiplied by target / applied: a reference m/z replaces a saved correction, and off undoes it. A reference m/z on a run whose "lockmass function" is the tail of a split raster (D7) is refused: that function is image data, not a reference.

The store records calibration.lock_mass_corrected as whether its m/z carry a correction, and a lock_mass block in the Waters-specific metadata: source (lmgt.inf or computed), reference_mz, tolerance_da, n_measurements, the correction range in ppm, and under undone a saved correction that was replaced or turned off.

Why. Measured on MSV000092638 (SYNAPT XS, MALDI, negative mode, 8,475 pixels, about three hours), against known brain lipid ions (PE 38:4, PS 40:6, PI 38:4, SHexCer 42:2;O2):

m/z stored 0-20 min 80-100 min 160-180 min uncorrected (Thyra before this) +11.6 ppm +18.3 ppm +20.6 ppm corrected against P17- (526.5545) +1.8 ppm +1.8 ppm +1.2 ppm HDImaging's lock-mass-corrected export -2 to -4 ppm over the run

Uncorrected, an ion moves by 4 to 5 of the 2 mDa centroid bins between the first and last rows of the image.

The library's own correction call writes lmgt.inf into the folder it was opened on, and every later open of that folder applies it (measured). Calling it on the user's run would change what every later reader of the run sees, and fails on a read-only share, so it is only ever called on the copy. On the run above the copy is 7.6 MB, the measurement takes 2 to 5 s, and its factors equal those from a full copy of the run digit for digit. The interpolation reproduces the library's own application to 0.03 ppm, the float32 rounding of the stored values.

On a profile read the stored m/z equal what the library returns from a corrected copy of the whole run to 0.08 ppm, with identical intensities. On a centroid read they do not quite: the library centroids a corrected run again rather than scaling its centroids, and on four scans of the run above its list held 1 to 20 fewer of about 8,000 peaks, its strong peaks sat a median 1 to 2 ppm from the scaled ones, and its total intensity was 0.3 to 0.7% lower. Thyra stores the vendor centroids of the run scaled by the factor, which corrects the m/z by exactly the measured drift and leaves the peak list the one the run gives. The lipid accuracy is the same either way to 0.5 ppm.

The correction is not applied by default: the run does not name its reference ("Experiment Reference Compound Name: N/A" in _extern.inf), and the library's automatic correction declines it for that reason. A guessed reference that matches the wrong peak would shift every m/z, so the reference stays the user's statement, and the run says when one is missing.

The warning about an uncorrected run says what its reference scans show, and the store records the same under lock_mass.reference_scans. First, how far their strongest peak moved between the first and the last group of reference scans. That needs no identification; on the run above it is +10.9 ppm over 10 groups, against an 11.3 ppm spread of the library's own factors. Second, what the scans look like, named only when that is unambiguous: at least five red phosphorus cluster ions of the run's polarity within 50 ppm whose offsets spread no more than 3 ppm, or leucine enkephalin as the strongest peak. On the run above: red phosphorus, 17 ions, stored +15.5 ppm from theory, P17- (526.5545) suggested. The suggestion is printed, never applied. Recognising references automatically, and reading the reference from the acquisition method, are left for later.

What changes in a store. With a reference m/z, every m/z value. With off on a run with a saved correction, every m/z value. Omitted, nothing (the warning is new). The lock_mass block is new.

docs.title: D85. A pixel one Waters function acquired twice
docs.text:
Status: Implemented (2026-10-22).

Decision. When scans of one function report the same pixel:

  • if a scan of the lock-mass reference function was acquired between two of them, the earlier one was cut short by it and is left out; the pixel keeps the scan acquired after the break;
  • the scans left are complete acquisitions of the pixel, and it stores their mean, each scan weighing 1/n.

Pixels that scans of different converted functions share (two mass ranges or channels of one acquisition) are summed as before, and the grid warns about those only. The Waters-specific metadata records repeated_pixels: interrupted_scans_left_out (function, scan, pixel) and pixels_averaged (function, scans, pixel). The metadata's peak count leaves out the scans left out.

Why. On MSV000092638 the raster stops every 20.2 minutes for seven lock-mass scans, and the pixel it was on is acquired again after them. All nine first scans inside the raster hold 0 to 2% of a normal scan's ion current. Summing kept them as a few per cent of extra signal on nine pixels; HDImaging's export of the run leaves exactly those nine scans out. Two complete acquisitions of one pixel (issue #233: two scans 40 ms apart on a 100 um MALDI set) were summed, so the pixel came out up to twice as bright as its neighbours; the mean keeps it on their scale.

What changes in a store. The intensities of the pixels concerned, and the metadata's peak count. Every other pixel is unchanged.

def summed_table(store):
    """The MSI table of a store, as opposed to its sibling tables."""
    key = next(k for k in store.tables if not k.endswith(("_mobility", "_msms")))
    return key, store.tables[key]


def ion_image(table, values):
    """Lay one value per pixel out on the acquisition grid."""
    x = table.obs["x"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    y = table.obs["y"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    image = np.full((y.max() + 1, x.max() + 1), np.nan)
    image[y, x] = values
    return image

docs.title: Explore a Thyra Dataset¶
docs.text:
This notebook shows how to read Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) data from a SpatialData store produced by Thyra.

For installation and the conversion step that produces such a store, see the Tutorial. This notebook picks up from its output.

Topics covered:

  • Loading a SpatialData zarr dataset
  • Accessing TIC (Total Ion Current) images
  • Accessing optical images and MSI-optical overlay
  • Accessing the average mass spectrum
  • Pixel counts and data representation
  • Accessing raw MSI data and pixel coordinates
  • Extracting ion images at specific m/z values
  • Working with 3D data and z-slices
  • Ion mobility: the axis, the mass-mobility heatmap, the grid table
  • Tandem MS: the isolation schedule and the demultiplexed sibling table

Runs with no configuration. If you have no dataset yet, the setup cell below generates a small synthetic one and converts it, so every cell can be executed as-is. To use your own data instead, set the THYRA_TUTORIAL_ZARR environment variable before starting Jupyter.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text:
The cell below resolves which dataset to open:

  1. THYRA_TUTORIAL_ZARR, if that environment variable is set
  2. otherwise example_data/synthetic_brain.zarr, generating and converting it on first run

Generating and converting the synthetic dataset takes a few seconds and needs no vendor SDK, so it works on Windows, macOS and Linux alike.

Note that convert_msi() called without a resampling_config keeps the original m/z axis, whereas the thyra command-line tool resamples by default. Everything below works either way -- only the number of columns in the table differs.

docs.title: SpatialData Structure Overview¶
docs.text:
A Thyra-converted dataset contains:

Element Key pattern Description Table {dataset_id}_z{i} AnnData table with intensity matrix (pixels x m/z), coordinates in .obs, m/z axis in .var, average spectrum in .uns TIC Image {dataset_id}_z{i}_tic 2D image of total ion current per pixel, shape (c, y, x) with c=1 Pixel Shapes {dataset_id}_z{i}_pixels GeoDataFrame with pixel geometries Optical Image {dataset_id}_optical_{suffix} Microscopy image (if available)

{i} is the slice number, so a 2D dataset has _z0: with the default dataset_id the keys are msi_dataset_z0, msi_dataset_z0_tic and msi_dataset_z0_pixels. A dataset converted with --handle-3d drops the _z{i} part and holds all slices in one table.

docs.title: Accessing TIC Images¶
docs.text: The TIC image represents the sum of all intensities across the mass spectrum for each pixel.

docs.title: Accessing Optical Images¶
docs.text:
When converted with include_optical=True, Thyra stores microscopy images alongside the MSI data. Keys follow the pattern {dataset_id}_optical_{suffix} where suffix is highres, derived, or derived from the filename.

Optical images and MSI-to-optical alignment come from vendor metadata, so they are present for Bruker acquisitions and absent for plain imzML input -- including the synthetic example dataset. The next few cells therefore print a notice instead of a figure unless you are pointing at a Bruker conversion. See Tutorial, Part 2 for a dataset that exercises this path.

docs.title: Overlaying MSI Data on Optical Image¶
docs.text: The optical image typically shows the full slide (e.g. multiple tissue sections), while the TIC only covers the measured region. Thyra stores an Affine transform on the TIC image that maps its raster indices into the optical image's pixel coordinate space. We extract this transform and use it to place the TIC at the correct position on the optical.

docs.title: Accessing the Average Mass Spectrum¶
docs.text: The average spectrum is the mean intensity across all non-empty pixels for each m/z value. It is stored in the .uns attribute of the main data table.

docs.title: Pixel Count and Data Representation¶
docs.text: MSI data is stored in a rectangular grid, but not all grid positions contain measurements. The TIC image makes it easy to distinguish data pixels from empty ones.

docs.title: Accessing Raw MSI Data¶
docs.text: The intensity matrix is stored as a sparse matrix in the AnnData table. Each row is one pixel, each column is one m/z bin.

docs.title: Extracting Ion Images¶
docs.text:
To visualise the spatial distribution of a specific m/z value, extract the corresponding intensities from the matrix and reshape them into image coordinates.

The cell below starts from the most intense peak in the average spectrum, which is guaranteed to be a populated bin. To map an arbitrary target m/z, integrate over a tolerance window instead -- see Searching for a Specific m/z Value below.

docs.title: Searching for a Specific m/z Value¶
Recalculating TIC and Average Spectrum¶
docs.text: You can recompute TIC and average spectrum directly from the intensity matrix to verify the stored values.

docs.title: Working with 3D Data and Z-Slices¶
docs.text: For 3D datasets, Thyra stores each z-slice as a separate table and TIC image with _z{i} suffixes.

docs.title: Pixel Size and Dataset Metadata¶
docs.text: Pixel size and conversion metadata are stored in sdata.attrs (SpatialData-level attributes). Additional metadata (instrument info, acquisition params, etc.) is in the table's .uns.

docs.title: Ion Mobility¶
docs.text:
A Bruker timsTOF acquisition sweeps a mobility ramp at every pixel, and the MSI table above is always summed over it. The store says so, and a conversion asked for --mobility-grid also keeps the ramp:

Where What uns["mobility_axis"] the axis that was summed away: the 1/K0 of every TIMS scan, its unit and the vendor calibration uns["mobility_heatmap"] the dataset's mean mass-mobility frame, about 4,000 m/z bins x 256 mobility channels {table}_mobility a sibling table with one column per occupied (m/z bin, mobility channel), written with --mobility-grid

An imzML export without a mobility array -- the synthetic dataset above -- has none of them, so the cells below open a second store. Point THYRA_TUTORIAL_TIMS_ZARR at a timsTOF conversion of your own and THYRA_TUTORIAL_MSMS_ZARR at a PASEF MS/MS one; with neither set, the repository's synthetic TIMS fixture is converted here instead.

The outputs saved in this notebook come from two real acquisitions: a 20 um MALDI-2 timsTOF measurement of a biofilm (18,838 pixels) for mobility, and a 713-pixel PASEF MS/MS acquisition of a tissue section, 15 scheduled precursors, for the tandem-MS section below. The field-by-field contract is in Output Format.

docs.title: The axis that was summed away¶
docs.text: uns["mobility_axis"] is the ramp itself: one 1/K0 value per TIMS scan, from the vendor calibration, decreasing with scan number. It is a feature coordinate -- it never enters obs, a coordinate system or a transform. A source with no mobility dimension writes no block at all, so "summed over mobility" and "never had any" stay distinguishable.

docs.title: The mean mass-mobility frame¶
docs.text: uns["mobility_heatmap"] is every pixel's raw (m/z, mobility, intensity) points binned and averaged over pixels. It is the discovery surface: look at it to see whether mobility separates anything in this dataset before paying for a mobility-resolved table. The 256 mobility channels are the same 256 the grid table below uses, over the same edges, so a box drawn here maps onto grid channels by integer index.

docs.title: The heatmap and the mean spectrum are the same measurement¶
docs.text: Summing the heatmap over its mobility channels must give back the average spectrum, coarsened onto mz_edges. That holds exactly under the default --tdf-spectrum scan_sum, where both are built from the same raw scans. Under --tdf-spectrum vendor_centroid it does not: the vendor peak picker keeps only the current inside the peaks it picks, while the heatmap bins every raw point (Design Decisions).

docs.title: The mobility-resolved table¶
docs.text:
--mobility-grid bins every pixel's points onto one set of mobility channels shared across the conversion and writes {table}_mobility, where a column is an occupied (m/z bin, channel) pair. Its var["mz"] therefore repeats, so consumers must discriminate on "mobility" in var.columns and never on the element name; var["mz_index"] points back at the column of the MSI table the feature was summed into.

Two species at one m/z that separate in mobility are one column there and two here, which is the whole reason to ask for the table (Design Decisions says why it is opt in). The query below looks for such a case: among the strongest m/z bins, one whose channels hold two features at least 12 channels apart -- further apart than a TIMS peak is wide, so they are two features and not one peak's own tails.

docs.title: Tandem MS¶
docs.text:
An MS/MS imaging run measures fragments, so var["mz"] is fragment m/z and nothing about the axis says so. uns["msms_schedule"] is what says it: the MS level, the isolation windows, their collision energies, and -- on Bruker PASEF, where each precursor owns a slice of the mobility ramp -- the scan range each window occupied.

When a pixel's frame isolates several precursors, the stored spectrum sums all of them: it is a chimera and must not be read as any one precursor's fragment spectrum. Thyra says so at WARNING during conversion and, by default, also writes the split apart as {table}_msms (Design Decisions).

docs.title: One precursor's block¶
docs.text:
Each precursor's columns are a contiguous block, sorted by (precursor_mz, precursor_mobility, mz), and the block's row sums are its precursor ion image. Two precursors can legitimately share an m/z -- a method isolates one mass at two mobility positions to keep an isomer pair apart -- so the block identity is precursor_index, never a float comparison on precursor_mz, and precursor_index means nothing outside this one store: two samples align on (precursor_mz, precursor_mobility) (Output Format).

A column inside the block is one fragment's image. In the outputs saved here the strongest of them lies inside the isolation window itself -- an ion that reached the collision cell and survived it, which is ordinary in a fragment spectrum -- and the fragments below the window are far weaker.

docs.title: Which defaults produced this store¶
docs.text: The reading that produced the numbers above is recorded, not implied: processing names the spectrum the TDF reader took, and the versioned metadata block names both sibling tables. Every entry is argued on the Design Decisions page.

docs.title: Implementation Notes¶
docs.text:
Average spectrum is calculated using only non-empty pixels (those with at least one non-zero intensity). This prevents artificial dilution from empty grid positions.

TIC image orientation follows standard imaging convention: first axis is Y (rows, top to bottom), second is X (columns, left to right).

Sparse storage: MSI data is highly sparse. Keep data in sparse format when possible and avoid .toarray() on the full matrix for large datasets.

Loading: Use spatialdata.read_zarr() to load datasets. This returns a SpatialData object with lazy-loaded elements.

docs.title: For tool developers
docs.text:
This page is for authors of MSI analysis tools who want to read a Thyra store. It states what a store promises and what it does not. For a tour of everything a store holds, see Output format.

A Thyra store is a SpatialData store written as a Zarr folder. Its spectra are AnnData tables: one row per pixel, one column per m/z bin, the intensities in a sparse matrix. Its images, such as the TIC image, are OME-Zarr images.

docs.title: Read a store
docs.text:
With spatialdata:

import numpy as np
import spatialdata as sd

sdata = sd.read_zarr("sample.zarr")
table = sdata.tables["msi_dataset_z0"]       # one row per pixel
X = table.X                                  # scipy CSC matrix, pixels x m/z bins
mz = table.var["mz"].to_numpy()              # the mass axis, one value per column
x = table.obs["x"].to_numpy()                # raster column of each row
y = table.obs["y"].to_numpy()                # raster row of each row
tic = np.asarray(sdata.images["msi_dataset_z0_tic"])[0]   # (y, x)
print(table.uns["msi_metadata"]["schema_version"])

Without spatialdata, with anndata and zarr only:

import anndata as ad
import numpy as np
import zarr

root = zarr.open_group("sample.zarr", mode="r")
print(list(root["tables"]))                  # the table names
table = ad.io.read_zarr("sample.zarr/tables/msi_dataset_z0")
tic_group = root["images/msi_dataset_z0_tic"]
level = tic_group.attrs["ome"]["multiscales"][0]["datasets"][0]["path"]
tic = np.asarray(tic_group[level])[0]        # (y, x)

Read the image's level path from its OME metadata, as above. Do not assume its name.

The default dataset id is msi_dataset. In a 2D conversion the first table is msi_dataset_z0 and its TIC image is msi_dataset_z0_tic. Users can change the id, so list the tables rather than hard-coding a name. The snippets on this page use the default names to stay short.

A 3D conversion (--handle-3d) differs: the table is msi_dataset, obs gains z, and the TIC image is a volume of shape (c, z, y, x). The snippets on this page assume a 2D store. See Output format.

docs.title: The rules a tool can rely on
Which table is which
docs.text:
A store can hold three kinds of table. Tell them apart by their var columns, never by the element name:

def table_kind(table):
    if "mobility" in table.var.columns:
        return "mobility"      # one column per (m/z, mobility) pair
    if "precursor_mz" in table.var.columns:
        return "msms"          # one column block per precursor
    return "msi"               # one column per m/z bin

No table carries both columns.

MSI table Mobility table MS/MS table Marked by neither column mobility in var precursor_mz in var var["mz"] strictly increasing, unique non-decreasing, repeats restarts at every precursor Sorted by mz (mz, mobility) (precursor_mz, precursor_mobility, mz) Unique key of a column mz (mz, mobility) (precursor_index, mz) Other var columns none today mz_index, mobility_index, ccs precursor_index, mz_index, precursor_mobility

Only the MSI table has a unique, strictly increasing var["mz"]. Code that binary-searches the mass axis must only be given the MSI table.

ccs is present on a mobility table whose axis is 1/K0. It is the collision cross section in square angstroms, for an assumed charge of 1; uns["ccs"] records the assumptions.

precursor_mobility is present only when the source states the precursors' mobility. Without it, the MS/MS table is sorted by (precursor_mz, mz). A reader may add other var columns to the MSI table, such as a native flight-time axis, so do not assume mz is the only one.

docs.title: How the tables connect
docs.text:
• A sibling table has the same rows as its MSI table, in the same order, with the same obs.
  • mz_index is the column of the MSI table that a sibling feature belongs to. Use it to relate the two mass axes. On a mobility table read from a continuous imzML, a feature outside the MSI table's mass range is given the first or last column.
  • The MSI table names its siblings in its metadata block: uns["msi_metadata"]["ms_analysis"]["ion_mobility"]["resolved_table"] and uns["msi_metadata"]["ms_analysis"]["fragmentation"]["resolved_table"]. Each key is absent when there is no such table.
  • precursor_index identifies a precursor within one store only. Two precursors can share an m/z (an isomer pair), so select by precursor_index. To match precursors across stores, compare precursor_mz and precursor_mobility within a tolerance.

docs.title: Rows and values
docs.text:
• obs["x"] and obs["y"] are integer raster positions. They need not start at 0. Rows follow the raster, left to right and top to bottom. obs["acquisition_order"], when present, gives the time order.
  • obs["spatial_x"] and obs["spatial_y"] are in micrometres. When the source states no pixel size, 1 µm is assumed, and uns["msi_metadata"]["provenance"]["pixel_size_source"] is "default".
  • A position the instrument never measured has no row. A position measured twice has one row holding the sum of both spectra.
  • X is stored as CSC on every route, with sorted row indices in each column. Every stored value is finite and non-negative. Zeros are not stored.
  • The var and obs column names in the metadata schema are reserved. They are never reused with a different meaning.

docs.title: What thyra validate checks
docs.text:
thyra validate sample.zarr exits with status 1 when a table breaks its rule, so it can gate a pipeline. It reads only var and the metadata blocks, never the matrix.

Table Checked every table var["mz"] present, numeric and finite; a valid uns["msi_metadata"] block MSI table mz strictly increasing; it matches the mass axis fingerprint, when one is recorded Mobility table mz non-decreasing; (mz, mobility) pairs unique and sorted MS/MS table precursor_mz non-decreasing; each precursor_index is one contiguous block; mz strictly increasing inside each block any table with ccs ccs numeric, finite, positive and as long as mz

docs.title: What is stable, and how changes are versioned
Versioned: the metadata block
docs.text:
Thyra writes uns["msi_metadata"] in every table, and it stays at that location. If Thyra cannot build the block, it logs a warning and writes none; thyra validate then fails the store. The block's schema_version follows semantic versioning:

  • Adding an optional field raises the minor version.
  • Renaming, removing or retyping a field, or making one required, raises the major version.
  • A validator for major version N rejects other majors, accepts older minors and warns on newer ones.

Each schema version from 0.6.0 on is published as JSON Schema at a fixed address, for example https://M4i-Imaging-Mass-Spectrometry.github.io/thyra/schema/0.13.0/msi_metadata.schema.json. A published version is never edited, and there is no latest. The same file ships inside the thyra package. See Metadata schema.

docs.title: Versioned: the package
docs.text:
The thyra package version follows semantic versioning, set from the commit messages. A new feature makes a minor release, and a fix or a speed-up makes a patch release. Only a change marked as breaking makes a major release.

The package version does not version the store's contents. A minor or patch release can change stored values, for example when a default changes or a wrong value is fixed. Read the changelog before you upgrade, not only for a major release. Design decisions gives the reason behind each default.

To see what made a store:

  • uns["msi_metadata"]["provenance"]["thyra_version"] is the Thyra version that wrote it. Note which versions your tool is tested against.
  • json.loads(uns["msi_metadata"]["processing"]) lists the processing steps and their parameters. The list is stored as a JSON string.
  • uns["msi_metadata"]["ms_analysis"]["spectrum_representation"] is "profile" or "centroid": what the reader delivered. It is absent when the source does not say.
  • uns["msi_metadata"]["provenance"]["mass_axis"] is a SHA-256 of the MSI table's var["mz"], with its length. Two stores with equal values share the same mass axis, bin for bin. Sibling tables carry their MSI table's value. See design decision D42.

docs.title: Not promised
docs.text:
• Element names. The dataset id is a user setting. Find tables by their columns and by resolved_table.
  • The mass axis. The default axis follows the acquisition's mass range, so two stores usually differ. Compare the fingerprint, or var["mz"] itself, before reading across stores.
  • The sibling feature axes. In a mobility grid table (--mobility-grid) and in an MS/MS table, only features that carry signal become columns. Two conversions with the same settings can give different var.
  • Other uns blocks, such as mobility_axis, mobility_heatmap and msms_schedule. They are described in Output format but carry no version of their own.
  • The source's own vocabulary. format_specific, acquisition_params, instrument_info and raw_metadata keep what the source said, so their keys differ by format.
  • Zarr storage details, such as chunk sizes and compression.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: The recipes below run as written against stores converted from the test fixtures in the Thyra repository.

docs.title: An ion image
docs.text:
Sum the columns inside an m/z window. On a resampled axis the bins are narrow, so a single bin is usually empty.

import numpy as np
import spatialdata as sd


def ion_image(table, target_mz, half_width):
    mz = table.var["mz"].to_numpy()          # MSI table only: strictly increasing
    lo, hi = np.searchsorted(mz, [target_mz - half_width, target_mz + half_width])
    values = np.asarray(table.X[:, lo:hi].sum(axis=1)).ravel()
    x = table.obs["x"].to_numpy()
    y = table.obs["y"].to_numpy()
    image = np.full((y.max() + 1, x.max() + 1), np.nan)   # NaN = not measured
    image[y, x] = values
    return image


sdata = sd.read_zarr("sample.zarr")
image = ion_image(sdata.tables["msi_dataset_z0"], 600.25, 0.05)

docs.title: A mobility window
docs.text:
Select the m/z window on the MSI table, then keep the mobility table's features inside it whose mobility falls in a range.

import numpy as np
import spatialdata as sd

sdata = sd.read_zarr("sample.zarr")
msi = sdata.tables["msi_dataset_z0"]
name = msi.uns["msi_metadata"]["ms_analysis"]["ion_mobility"]["resolved_table"]
mob = sdata.tables[name]

mz = msi.var["mz"].to_numpy()
lo, hi = np.searchsorted(mz, [600.25 - 0.05, 600.25 + 0.05])
mz_index = mob.var["mz_index"].to_numpy()
mobility = mob.var["mobility"].to_numpy()        # 1/K0 for TIMS

selected = (mz_index >= lo) & (mz_index < hi) & (mobility >= 1.3) & (mobility < 1.4)
values = np.asarray(mob.X[:, selected].sum(axis=1)).ravel()   # one value per pixel

On a timsTOF grid table with the default settings, the same window over all mobility values gives the MSI table's ion image. uns["mobility_marginal"]["current_ratio"] on the grid table records how closely the two tables agree.

docs.title: A precursor block
docs.text:
Look the precursor up once, then select its block by precursor_index. Never compare precursor_mz with ==.

import numpy as np
import spatialdata as sd

sdata = sd.read_zarr("sample.zarr")
msi = sdata.tables["msi_dataset_z0"]
name = msi.uns["msi_metadata"]["ms_analysis"]["fragmentation"]["resolved_table"]
msms = sdata.tables[name]

precursor_mz = msms.var.groupby("precursor_index")["precursor_mz"].first()
index = (precursor_mz - 500.0).abs().idxmin()  # nearest precursor to m/z 500
# Two precursors can share an m/z: then compare precursor_mobility as well.

block = (msms.var["precursor_index"] == index).to_numpy()
fragment_mz = msms.var["mz"].to_numpy()[block]
precursor_image = np.asarray(msms.X[:, block].sum(axis=1)).ravel()  # per pixel
fragment_images = msms.X[:, block]           # one column per fragment

uns["demultiplexed_current"]["current_ratio"] on the MS/MS table says how much of the MSI table's ion current the blocks hold together.

docs.title: Do two stores share a mass axis?
docs.text:
import spatialdata as sd


def mass_axis(path):
    table = sd.read_zarr(path).tables["msi_dataset_z0"]
    return table.uns["msi_metadata"]["provenance"].get("mass_axis")


a, b = mass_axis("first.zarr"), mass_axis("second.zarr")
same_axis = a is not None and a == b

A store without the field predates the fingerprint. Compare var["mz"] directly for those.

docs.title: Your first conversion
docs.text:
Converting a dataset takes one command: thyra, then your data, then a name for the result.

thyra your_data result.zarr

This page shows each part. You need Thyra installed first: see Install.

docs.title: Step 1: Find your data
docs.text:
Point Thyra at the file or folder your instrument wrote:

Your instrument Point Thyra at Bruker timsTOF or solariX the folder ending in .d Bruker rapifleX the folder that holds the .dat, _poslog.txt and _info.txt files Waters (MassLynx) the folder ending in .raw PHI nanoTOF (ToF-SIMS) the file ending in .raw Any instrument that exports imzML the .imzML file, with its .ibd file next to it mzPeak (experimental) the .mzpeak file

What each instrument needs, and which computers can read it: Which files can I convert?

No data at hand? This command makes a small example dataset to practise on:

thyra-example-data example_data/synthetic_brain.imzML

docs.title: Step 2: Convert
docs.text:
Type thyra, then the path to your data, then a name for the result ending in .zarr:

thyra "D:\MSI\brain section 1.d" brain_section_1.zarr

Three tips:

  • Put quotes around a path that contains spaces, as above.
  • Drag and drop. Drag your data from the file browser onto the terminal window, and its full path appears. This saves typing it.
  • The result goes to the folder your terminal is in, which is shown before the cursor. To save it somewhere else, give a full path, such as "D:\MSI\brain_section_1.zarr".

Thyra prints its progress as it works. When it is done, the last line says:

Conversion completed successfully. Output stored at brain_section_1.zarr

Small datasets take seconds. Large ones can take several minutes.

docs.title: Step 3: Check the result
docs.text:
A new folder, brain_section_1.zarr, is your converted dataset. It appears under that name only once it is finished. Keep the folder whole: copy or move it like any other folder, but do not take files out of it.

Next: look at the result.

docs.title: Common situations
docs.text: Most datasets need nothing more than the command above. These are the exceptions you are most likely to meet.

docs.title: Your folder holds several datasets
docs.text:
Point Thyra at a folder that holds several .d datasets, and it lists them and asks which one to convert:

Found 3 datasets in slide_folder:
  [1] C1501.d
  [2] E2501.d
  [3] E2506.d

Select dataset to convert: 3

Type the number and press Enter. A script cannot answer, so there Thyra stops and names the datasets. Give it one .d folder instead, or pipe the number in, for example echo 3 | thyra slide_folder out.zarr. A folder that holds only one dataset is converted without a question.

docs.title: Your acquisition has several regions
docs.text:
Thyra converts all regions of a Bruker timsTOF slide into one result. To convert only one, add --region and the region's name as flexImaging shows it:

thyra data.d region_03.zarr --region 03

Thyra lists the regions it finds when it starts, so a first run shows you the names.

docs.title: Thyra cannot find the pixel size
docs.text:
Most files record their pixel size. If yours does not, Thyra stops before it writes anything and tells you so. Run it again with --pixel-size and the size in micrometres:

thyra input.imzML output.zarr --pixel-size 50

docs.title: You do not want the optical image
docs.text: Bruker acquisitions often include a photo of the slide, and Thyra adds it to the result. To leave it out, add --no-optical.

docs.title: You want the original m/z values
docs.text:
Thyra puts every spectrum on one shared m/z axis, because most analysis tools need that. To keep each spectrum's own m/z values instead, add --no-resample.

Advanced: How Thyra chooses the shared m/z axis

This step is called resampling. Thyra looks at the instrument type and the data to choose the spacing of the axis and the method that moves each peak onto it. You can set the method, the spacing and the mass range yourself. Resampling explains each choice and when to change it.

docs.title: You have a 3D dataset
docs.text:
Thyra saves each slice as its own 2D dataset. To keep them together as one 3D volume, add --handle-3d.

Every other option is explained, one task at a time, in Change how Thyra converts.

docs.title: Convert from Python
docs.text:
Advanced: Use Thyra inside a Python script or notebook

The same conversion is one function call:

from thyra import convert_msi

convert_msi("brain_section_1.d", "brain_section_1.zarr")

It takes the same options as the command, such as pixel_size_um=50. One difference: from Python, resampling is off unless you turn it on. The Python API lists every argument.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text: Troubleshooting lists the common errors and how to fix each one.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
• Change how Thyra converts: the common options, explained.
  • Command-line options: every option, with examples.
  • Output format: everything inside the .zarr folder.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Words you will meet in these pages, in plain language. The computer terms come first, then the mass spectrometry ones.

docs.title: Computer terms
docs.text: Terminal A window where you type commands. On Windows it is called PowerShell; on macOS and Linux, Terminal. Command A line you type into the terminal and run with Enter, such as thyra --version. Path The address of a file or folder, such as /Volumes/data/MSI/brain.d on macOS. On Windows, a path starts with a drive letter, such as D:. Python The programming language Thyra is written in. You need it installed, but you do not need to write any. pip Python's standard installer for packages such as Thyra. uv A fast installer for Python programs. It can also fetch the right version of Python for you. Environment A separate set of Python packages, so that the packages of one project do not interfere with another's. Tools such as conda and uv create them. Jupyter notebook A document that mixes text with Python code you can run piece by piece. The Explore the result in Python page is one. SpatialData An open format and Python library for spatial data from biology, such as imaging mass spectrometry. Thyra saves your data in this format. Zarr The way SpatialData stores data on disk: a folder of many small files that programs can read a piece at a time. That is why the result is a folder ending in .zarr. Table (AnnData) The part of the result that holds the spectra: one row per pixel, one column per m/z bin. AnnData is the name of the Python format for such tables. scverse A community of open-source Python tools for single-cell and spatial biology. SpatialData, napari-spatialdata, scanpy and squidpy belong to it. napari A free image viewer. With the napari-spatialdata plugin, it opens SpatialData results. Command-line option An extra instruction added to a command, starting with --, such as --pixel-size 50.

docs.title: Mass spectrometry terms
docs.text: MSI (mass spectrometry imaging) Recording a mass spectrum at every point of a sample, so that each m/z value can be shown as an image. m/z Mass-to-charge ratio, the x-axis of a mass spectrum. Spectrum The intensities measured at one pixel, across the m/z range. Pixel size The distance between neighbouring measurement points, in micrometres. TIC (total ion current) The sum of all intensities in one spectrum. A TIC image shows it for every pixel, and gives a quick overview of the sample. Ion image An image of the intensity of one m/z value, or a narrow range around it, across all pixels. Profile and centroid data Profile data records the full shape of each peak. Centroid data keeps one point per peak. Resampling and m/z bins Instruments record each spectrum at slightly different m/z values. Resampling moves every spectrum onto one shared set of m/z positions, called bins, so that the same column means the same m/z in every pixel. Region A separately defined area of an acquisition, for example one tissue section on a slide that holds several. Optical image A photo or microscope scan of the slide, taken before the measurement. Teaching points Marks that link positions in the optical image to positions of the instrument's stage. Thyra uses them to lay the MSI data over the photo. imzML An open file format for imaging mass spectrometry. It comes as two files: an .imzML file that describes the data and an .ibd file that holds the numbers. Ion mobility (TIMS) A separation of ions by their size and shape, in addition to m/z. Bruker timsTOF instruments measure it with trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS). 1/K0 The unit of ion mobility on a timsTOF: the inverse reduced mobility, in V s/cm2. Larger ions of the same charge have a larger 1/K0. Mass-mobility heatmap A picture of the whole image in two dimensions: m/z against mobility. Two spots at one m/z but at different mobility are two different ions. CCS (collision cross section) A size measure of an ion, worked out from its mobility. The mobility table holds it in the column ccs, in square angstroms. Thyra assumes each ion has charge 1. MS/MS Tandem mass spectrometry: selected ions are broken into fragments, and the fragments are measured. Precursor and fragment In MS/MS, the precursor is the ion the instrument selects. The fragments are the pieces it breaks into. PASEF and iprm-PASEF Bruker timsTOF methods that select precursors one after the other as they leave the mobility separation. In imaging, iprm-PASEF fragments the same list of precursors at every pixel.

docs.title: imzML Parser Notes
docs.text:
Thyra reads imzML through pyimzML 1.5.5. This page is the written-down half of a survey of everything Thyra relies on from that library: hazards that are real and verified, but that correctly get no code today — because they are unreachable from Thyra's current call graph, because the safe thing is already what Thyra does, or because the surface in question is one Thyra deliberately does not use.

Nothing here is a bug report against the shipped converter. It is the set of things that would cost somebody a day if they had to rediscover them, listed where a future reader will look before making the change that reaches them.

docs.title: ImzMLParser is not thread-safe
docs.text:
ImzMLParser.get_spectrum_as_string does two unsynchronised seek-then-read pairs on a single shared file handle:

self.m.seek(offsets[0])
mz_string = self.m.read(lengths[0])
self.m.seek(offsets[1])
intensity_string = self.m.read(lengths[1])

Two threads interleaving between a seek and its read get each other's bytes. Measured over real pea.imzML, eight threads sharing one parser, 2000 getspectrum calls:

corrupt reads 108 (5.4%) exceptions raised 0 corrupt at the correct declared length 84 of 108 corrupt with mz.size == 0 24 corrupt reads with a threading.Lock added 0 of 2000

The 84 are the dangerous ones: the array comes back the length the header promised, holding another pixel's masses. No length check, emptiness check or dtype check can see it.

This is not a live defect. Thyra's imzML reads are strictly serial — a grep for concurrency primitives across thyra/ finds three hits, all of them on the class registry and the Bruker buffer pool, none on the imzML read path, and a non-blocking-lock proxy over two real conversions confirmed no contention ever occurs.

It is written down because parallelising the imzML read is an obvious future optimisation, and this trap is laid directly underneath it. The sanctioned route is parser.portable_spectrum_reader() with one open file object per worker, never a shared ImzMLParser.

docs.title: Do not "fix" the .ibd resolution to match pyimzml
docs.text:
There are two rules for finding the .ibd beside an imzML, and Thyra's is the more robust of the two. This section exists because the asymmetry looks, at a glance, like Thyra being sloppy.

Thyra (production)pyimzml (_infer_bin_filename) 
self.ibd_path = imzml_path.with_suffix(".ibd")
if not self.ibd_path.exists():
    raise ValueError(...)
self.ibd_file = open(self.ibd_path, mode="rb")

ibd_path = [f for f in imzml_path.parent.glob('*')
            if re.match(r'.+\.ibd', str(f), re.IGNORECASE)
            and f.stem == imzml_path.stem][0]

pyimzml's re.IGNORECASE is decorative: the f.stem == imzml_path.stem comparison sitting beside it is a plain case-sensitive ==. So the flag buys nothing, and three ordinary situations behave worse under pyimzml's rule:

Situation pyimzml Thyra SAMPLE.IBD beside sample.imzML IndexError: list index out of range resolves — Path.exists() is case-insensitive on Windows A parent directory named proj.ibd the unanchored regex matches the full path, so every same-stem sibling qualifies — including the imzML itself, which is what gets returned unaffected; only the .ibd suffix is ever constructed A half-finished download sample.ibdtmp .+\.ibd matches it, so it competes with the real file unaffected

Do not change with_suffix('.ibd').exists() to match pyimzml

It would be a regression on all three rows. If the resolution rule ever does need to change, it should get stricter, not more like _infer_bin_filename.

A related consequence worth knowing when writing tests: production always passes ibd_file= explicitly, so it never reaches _infer_bin_filename at all. Tests that construct a bare ImzMLParser(path) are exercising a rule the shipped code does not use, which means they cannot catch a resolution bug in it. Use tests.fixtures.imzml_parser.production_parser instead; it mirrors ImzMLReader._initialize_parser exactly.

Two smaller traps on the same handle:

  • ibd_file=None is not the same as omitting the argument. Omitting it infers the path; passing None gives a parser that raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'seek' on the first read. A caller writing ibd_file=maybe_handle gets the unreadable parser whenever the handle is None.
  • __enter__/__exit__ close a handle the parser does not own. With ibd_file=f supplied, parser.m is f, and leaving a with block closes the caller's file. Thyra does not use with on a parser; ImzMLReader.close() already closes the same aliased handle twice, which is idempotent in CPython and load-bearing on nothing.

docs.title: Dead pyimzml surface, for anyone tempted to adopt it
docs.text: None of the following is reachable from Thyra today. All of it looks useful, and all of it is broken in a way that would not be obvious on first use.

docs.title: _bisect_spectrum returns the first peak for any query below the range
docs.text:
ix_l, ix_u = bisect_left(mzs, mz_value - tol), bisect_right(mzs, mz_value + tol) - 1
if ix_l == len(mzs):
    return len(mzs), len(mzs)
if ix_u < 1:
    return 0, 0          # <-- "nothing matched" and "peak 0 matched" are the same answer

Query below the mass range and bisect_right returns 0, so ix_u is -1, so the function reports the half-open range (0, 0) — which the caller reads as peak zero matched. Measured: getionimage(bellini, mz=0.5, tol=0.05) returns a 128x128 image with 16384 of 16384 pixels non-zero, where the truth is a blank image.

getionimage also constructs a UserWarning about z=0 and never raises it — UserWarning("...") on a line by itself is just an allocated object.

docs.title: browse() hands back bare map objects
docs.text: _SpectrumMetaDataBrowser._find_referenceable_param_groups ends with ids = map(...); return ids. Anything that indexes the result, checks its length, or iterates it a second time sees an exhausted iterator rather than an error.

docs.title: check_peaks_overlap is not a centroid/profile tiebreaker
docs.text:
Two independent reasons not to adopt it:

  1. It calls random.seed(42) on the global random module, clobbering the caller's RNG stream as a side effect of asking a question about a file. calc_statistics does the same.
  2. On real bellini.imzML — which declares MS:1000128 profile spectrum — it returns 0.01% overlap, i.e. it says centroid. Adopting it would put Thyra in disagreement with a shipped file's own declaration on day one.

docs.title: include_spectra_metadata='full' is infeasible, not merely expensive
docs.text:
It appends a SpectrumData object per spectrum. Measured at +147 MiB per 12,737 spectra, which extrapolates to roughly 10.6 GiB on the 918,855-spectrum xenium file — on top of the parse. The list mode is cheaper and does not work either: it never follows referenceableParamGroupRef, so it returns None for every spectrum, with no signal that the lookup was structurally incapable of succeeding. That is exactly where SCiLS puts MS:1000127.

The list mode also matches on the accession alone. pyimzml's ACCESSION_FIX_MAPPING turns a mislabelled pair such as MS:1000128 named "positive scan" into MS:1000130, but only where it parses terms itself: fileContent and the parameter groups. On a spectrum the pair stated no polarity at all. Thyra's _pyimzml_compat.ensure_spectrum_term_fix applies the same correction to the per-spectrum values (D55).

The MS level is not asked for through include_spectra_metadata at all. The pyimzml writer states MS:1000511 in the spectrum1 group, as does mzpeak-convert's imzML input, so the list mode would give None for every spectrum of such a file. _pyimzml_compat.ensure_spectrum_check reads it in the same per-spectrum step instead: the spectrum's own term first, then the groups it references (the last one listed that states a level, as pyimzml's full mode resolves them). It costs a loop over the spectrum's direct children, one byte per spectrum on the parser, and nothing more (D73).

docs.title: Two more constraints worth not rediscovering
docs.text:
• choose_iterparse validates nothing. "LXML", "elementtree", "expat" and "" all fall through to ElementTree without complaint. Thyra's parse_lib="ElementTree" pin is therefore protected by exact string equality and nothing else — a typo would be silent, and here it would be harmless because the fallback happens to be the pinned choice. Do not rely on that staying true. The reason for the pin is in the comment block at ImzMLReader._initialize_parser.
  • SIZE_DICT and numpy disagree about 'l'. PRECISION_DICT['64-bit integer'] is 'l' and SIZE_DICT['l'] is 8, but np.dtype('l').itemsize is 4 on Windows and 8 on Linux, so the same file decodes differently on the two platforms. If this ever needs fixing, patch the module globals — set PRECISION_DICT['64-bit integer'] = 'q' and SIZE_DICT['q'] = 8. Patching the per-instance parser.sizeDict is not enough: PortableSpectrumReader reads the module-level dict, so the same parser would report one size from getspectrum and another from its own portable_spectrum_reader.

docs.title: The coordinate base is not a constant
docs.text:
The specification numbers x and y from 1, and pyimzml passes through whatever the document holds. Exports numbered from 0 exist, so subtracting a constant 1 would put the first column of one at x = -1. A negative index is a legal negative numpy index, so the converter's grid guard would drop those spectra rather than crash: a 3x3 acquisition at coordinates 0..2 previewed as grid (2, 2), warned that "5 spectra sat outside the declared 2x2x1 grid", stored 4 rows and exited 0.

The base is now measured, by thyra.utils.imzml_coordinate_base, and the rule is deliberately not the one z uses:

axis rule why x, y min(observed_minimum, 1) 0 folds down; 1 and anything above it keep the spec base z observed_minimum z has no physical origin to preserve

Rebasing x and y on their observed minimum would move a legitimately cropped acquisition. A file whose leftmost occupied column is x = 5 is a region of a larger slide, not a 0-based export, and nothing in the document distinguishes the two; sliding it to the origin would change its grid width, every obs["spatial_x"], the TIC image extent and its pixel footprint. Folding only a 0 down leaves every such file exactly where it was.

The declared IMS:1000042 / IMS:1000043 pixel counts were the third candidate and are not used for the base. A conversion never reads them. The header-only preview reports them as the grid, but only when they fit the declared spectrum count and the first spectrum is at x and y of 1 or more (D65).

The file's own coordinate of index 0 on each axis is reported as EssentialMetadata.coordinate_offsets and written to coordinate_systems.global.coordinate_offsets_px, so a store can say where its origin came from. Before this the imzML extractor set no offsets at all.

One exception, on z. pyimzml gives a spectrum without IMS:1000052 the z of 1. That 1 is subtracted, so the spectra sit on plane 0, but the store records a z offset of 0, as every format without z does (D30).

Whether a file states z is judged on every spectrum, during the parser's own pass (D63). A spectrum states z when its scan carries IMS:1000052 itself, with a value. A file states z on every spectrum or on none. A file that mixes the two is refused with the mzPeak route's sentence. So is a file whose scans take z from a parameter group: pyimzml does not read it there, and gives those spectra its stand-in 1. It used to read the first spectrum only, so the recorded offset depended on which spectrum came first.

Pinned by tests/unit/readers/test_imzml_zero_based.py, which converts a 0-based file, a 1-based one and a cropped 1-based one -- the last being the file the rejected alternative would have moved.

docs.title: Fixed in Thyra, still true of pyimzml
docs.text:
One finding was real enough to grow code: imzmldict discards unitAccession. convert_cv_param(accession, value) takes no unit argument, so __readimzmlmeta cannot carry one even though ParamGroup.cv_params preserves it. imzmldict['pixel size x'] is a bare number in whatever unit the vendor declared, so reading it as micrometres is wrong: a file declaring its pixel as 4406.25 nanometre (UO:0000018) would land on disk with obs/spatial_x a thousand times too large, and convert_msi would still return True.

The information is never lost from the document, only from the dict, so ImzMLMetadataExtractor reads the unit-bearing path — each cv_params tuple is (name, accession, value, raw_name, raw_value, unit_name, unit_accession) — and converts: UO:0000016 mm x1000, UO:0000017 um x1, UO:0000018 nm /1000. Any other declared unit is not read: a warning names the unit, the pixel size is left out, and a conversion asks for --pixel-size and converts at the size given, as the mzPeak route does. It used to be refused, so such a file could not be converted even with the flag. A cvParam with no unit at all keeps the historical micrometre reading, because real vendor files (the IONTOF class among them) write IMS:1000046 unitless and were being read correctly. The unit and the name are read from the cvParam that holds the value, including one in a parameter group the scan settings reference.

Corroboration that the ambiguity was genuine rather than theoretical: pyimzml's own get_physical_coordinates docstring says it returns nanometers while multiplying by the same unlabelled pixel size x that Thyra treats as micrometres. The library's author disagreed with Thyra about the unit.

The behaviour is pinned by tests/unit/readers/test_hand_authored_fixtures.py::TestUnitNanometre, whose assertions now state the correct conversion, and the unread unit, rather than characterise the error.

docs.title: IMS:1000046 was an area until 2017
docs.text:
Until commit 421481e of the imzML vocabulary (2017-09-07) IMS:1000046 was named "pixel size" and gave the area of a pixel, in an area unit. IMS:1000047 was "image shape" and had no value type. Since that commit the two are "pixel size (x)" and "pixel size y", both lengths, and "image shape" is IMS:1000058.

Public files still use the old form. In a header audit of public imzML files, 70 give IMS:1000046 and no IMS:1000047, and all 70 name it "pixel size". 39 of them also give a pixel count and an extent. In all 39, sqrt(value) x count is the extent exactly: value 10000, count 174, extent 17400 is a 100 um pixel. None of the 39 carries a unit. The other 31 declare UO:0000015, centimetre, and name it "micrometer".

pyimzml renames the term while parsing. It warns Accession IMS:1000046 found with incorrect name "pixel size", and puts the value in imzmldict['pixel size x']. The area is then a bare number under the name of a length. The name the file wrote survives as raw_name, the fourth field of the cv_params tuple.

Both routes to a pixel size ask for both terms, so a file with the lone term gave none. One form got through: the old name with a number on IMS:1000047. It was read as two lengths, 10000 um by 10000 um for a 100 um pixel, and convert_msi returned True. No such file was found. 28 public files that give both terms were read, one per deposit and writer, standing for 408, and the four real files at hand. All use the current names.

Thyra now reads raw_name, and does not read IMS:1000046 under the name "pixel size". The file gives no pixel size, the log says why, and the conversion asks for --pixel-size. The preview does the same, because the header-only extractor shares _extract_pixel_size_fast. _extract_pixel_size_from_xml has the same guard. It is never reached on a real file: pyimzml 1.5.5 keeps no root on its Metadata, so the method returns at its first check.

The mzPeak path goes further and tests the value against the pixel count and the extent, see design decision D27.

Pinned by tests/unit/metadata/extractors/test_imzml_old_pixel_size.py.

docs.title: How public files state the pixel size
docs.text:
The headers of the 479 public imzML files of that audit that state a pixel size were read again on 2026-09-29, for the unit. They come from two repositories and 15 deposits, and 380 of them from one writer. So the table says which forms occur, not how common each is.

The header gives Files Deposits Thyra takes both terms, unit micrometre 381 9 the values both terms, no unit 28 4 the values, as micrometres IMS:1000046 alone, named "pixel size", no unit 39 4 none, and asks for --pixel-size IMS:1000046 alone, named "pixel size", unit accession UO:0000015, unit name "micrometer" 31 1 none, and asks for --pixel-size

67 of the 479 give no unit. Reading a value without a unit as micrometres is an assumption. The file does not confirm it.

UO:0000015 is the centimetre. In the 31 files the accession and the name of the unit disagree, and nothing else in the header settles which one is meant.

Five synthetic test files hold these forms, one per row and one more for the area without an extent. Each is the same acquisition of 3 by 2 pixels of 50 um. They are in tests/data/fixtures/, with the script that writes them. From each of them Thyra takes 50 um or no pixel size, on the imzML path and on the mzPeak path.

Pinned by tests/unit/metadata/extractors/test_pixel_size_fixtures.py.

docs.title: IMS:1000080 is never checked against the .ibd header
docs.text:
The imzML specification puts the binary file's UUID in the first 16 bytes of the .ibd and the same value in the XML as IMS:1000080. pyimzml reads neither against the other -- it never touches the header bytes at all.

That pair is the only thing that can tell an .imzML apart from a different acquisition's .ibd renamed to sit beside it. Every other check Thyra makes (ImzMLReader._validate_parser_state) reads the XML's own offsets and lengths against the binary's size, which a wrong-but-similarly-shaped file satisfies.
